news.title: Map of States Trump Won Twice Where Democrats Lead With 2 Months to Midterm
news.text: Democrats are leading in several Senate and gubernatorial races in states President Donald Trump carried in both 2020 and 2024, according to recent polling released less than two months before the 2026 midterm elections. The competitive contests in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio, North Carolina and Texas are emerging as key tests of the political climate during Trump's second term, which has seen his approval rating slip amid concerns over the economy, tariff policies, and the ongoing Iran war. Democrats, meanwhile, are hoping to capitalize on the political climate, which includes recent Democratic wins and overperformance, and the fact that historically the party not in the White House performs better in the midterms, to make inroads in states Trump previously won. On Thursday, forecaster Sabato's Crystal Ball moved three gubernatorial contests toward Democrats, including races in Iowa and Alaska, states Trump won in 2020 and 2024. Other forecasters, like Cook Political Report, have rated the races as tossups as Democratic candidates continue to post competitive polling numbers ahead of November. With exactly two months until Election Day on November 3, the competitive races could help shape the balance of power in Washington and state capitals alike, as Democrats seek to erode Republican gains in some of Trump's strongest states. 2020 and 2024 Presidential Elections Trump won 25 states in the 2020 presidential election and 31 in 2024. In 2020, Trump lost to Democrat Joe Biden, who won 306 Electoral College votes to Trump's 232. Four years later, Trump defeated Democratic nominee Kamala Harris, winning 312 electoral votes to the vice president's 226 and reclaiming the White House. Trump's 2024 victory was aided by flipping six states that Biden won in 2020: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. The remaining 25 states voted for Trump in both elections and have generally formed the Republican Party's reliable presidential strongholds. Republicans also regained control of the Senate in 2024, flipping Democratic-held seats and securing a majority in the chamber, while maintaining control of the House of Representatives. At the state level, Republicans entered 2025 holding a majority of governorships nationwide. “At the end of the day, in 2024 Donald Trump was a rising tide lifting all Republican boats, but in 2026 he is a falling tide lowering all Republican boats from sea to shining sea," Mark Jones, a politics professor at Rice University, recently told Newsweek for a related story. The midterms are widely viewed as a key test of Trump's standing with voters since returning to office, as well as the political weight of his endorsements in competitive races. Iowa Governor’s Race Iowa was viewed as a battleground for much of the 2000s, with former President Barack Obama carrying the state by about 10 points in 2008 and 6 points in 2012. But Trump performed well in the state in each of his presidential bids, winning by 10 points in 2016, 8 points in 2020 and 13 points in 2024. Republican Governor Kim Reynolds, who has led the state since 2017, is not seeking reelection. The last time a Democrat won Iowa’s governorship was in 2006, when Chet Culver was elected. Culver lost his reelection in 2010 to Republican Terry Branstad, and Republicans have been in office ever since. Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand, a Democrat, is going up against Republican businessman Zach Lahn in the state's open governor's race. Political commentators have noted that Sand's name recognition may help push him across the finish line. An Emerson College Polling survey released on Thursday found Sand leading Lahn 49 percent to 46 percent, with 6 percent undecided. “Independent voters break for Sand over Lahn by a 12-point margin, 51% to 39%,” Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, said in the poll’s release. According to the poll’s crosstabs, about 30 people who voted for Trump in 2024 are backing Sand. Sand's lead comes as some voters appear poised to split their ballots between the two parties. Kimball said, “About six percent of voters in the Iowa poll are splitting their ticket to support both Republican Ashley Hinson for Senate and Democrat Rob Sand for Governor.” The poll of 750 likely voters was conducted between August 31 and September 1. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Other polls have also found Sand ahead. An August Suffolk University poll found Sand ahead of Lahn 48 percent to 44 percent among 500 likely Iowa voters, with 9 percent undecided. The survey, conducted August 20-23, has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. An Emerson College Polling survey found Sand at 48 percent, compared with Lahn at 43 percent. Two percent of respondents said they would vote for someone else, while 7 percent were still undecided. The survey polled 712 likely voters August 2-4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. A survey from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 600 likely voters June 15-27, showed Sand up a single point, 48 percent to 47 percent. A Fox News poll showed Sand up 9 points, 53 percent to 44 percent. Beach Research and Shaw & Company Research conducted it from June 23-27 among 1,003 registered voters. On Thursday, Sabato’s Crystal Ball upgraded the race from a toss-up to “leans Democratic.” The forecaster said in a Thursday update that Sand “has posted consistent, though sometimes small, polling leads," which impacted their rating. The Cook Political Report had previously updated the race to the leans Democratic on August 20, writing, “Sand has been running one of the strongest campaigns in the country this cycle, and he has opened up a consistent lead outside of the margin of error in both public and private polling.” Ohio “Ohio is the one to watch,” Matt Klink, owner and president of Klink Campaigns, told Newsweek last week, in reference to a potential Democratic pickup. Trump carried the state by about 11 percentage points in 2024, an improvement over his 2020 and 2016 performances, when he won by about 8 points each time. But Ohio was viewed as more competitive for Democrats not long before. Obama narrowly carried Ohio in 2008 and 2012. The Buckeye State is set for a busy election season, with competitive races for both governor and U.S. Senate on the ballot this November. Ohio Governor’s Race The state's most recent Democratic governor was Ted Strickland, who served from 2007 to 2011. Ohio has elected only Republican governors since then, including current Governor Mike DeWine, who won reelection in 2022 but is now term-limited. Democrat Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health who gained statewide prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic, faces Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate and DOGE member. Polls point to a close matchup. A Wedgewood Poll of 800 likely voters conducted between August 11 and 13 found a tight race for the governor’s mansion, with Acton ahead by 1 point, 47 percent to Ramaswamy’s 46 percent. Seven percent of the participants were undecided. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A Fox News poll conducted August 6 to 10 among 1,008 registered voters put Ramaswamy ahead, 50 percent to 48 percent. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Tulchin Research found Acton leading 46 percent to 44 percent in a survey sponsored by John Kulewicz, the Democratic candidate for Ohio attorney general. The survey, conducted July 29 to August 4 among 660 likely voters, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up after moving it from the Lean Republican column in a July update. Explaining the shift, the forecaster wrote that “it’s an inescapable law of politics: Money can only propel a campaign so far when its candidate’s flaws act as an anchor.” Ohio Senate Race The state's most recent Democratic senator was Sherrod Brown, who served from 2007 until his defeat by Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Brown is now seeking a return to the Senate in a 2026 race against Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the remainder of Vice President JD Vance's term. An August Fox News poll found Brown leading Husted by 8 points, 53 percent to 45 percent, with about 2 percent undecided. Brown leads among independents in Ohio by 38 points, 66 percent to 28 percent for Husted. The poll of 1,008 registered Ohio voters was conducted August 6-10. A Wedgewood Poll of 800 likely voters conducted between August 11 and 13 found Brown with 48 percent to Husted’s 44 percent. About 8 percent of voters were undecided. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball view the race as a toss-up. Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted it from Lean Republican earlier in June after Brown and Husted formally won their parties’ nominations. North Carolina Senate Race North Carolina has long been one of the nation's most closely watched battleground states, and voters are often known for ticket-splitting. Trump carried the state by about 1.3 percentage points over Biden in 2020 and expanded that margin to roughly 3.2 points against Harris in 2024. Despite Republicans' success at the presidential level, Democrats have won statewide races. The last Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from North Carolina was Kay Hagan, who defeated Republican incumbent Elizabeth Dole in 2008. Since then, Republicans have held both Senate seats. The race is for the seat currently held by Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who is not seeking reelection. Roy Cooper, who served as North Carolina governor from 2017 through 2024, is seeking a return to elected office, but this time in the Senate, while Republican Michael Whatley is the former chairman of the Republican National Committee (RNC) and the North Carolina Republican Party. A recent High Point University poll found Cooper leading Whatley 50 percent to 45 percent, a 5-point advantage that falls within the poll’s 5.2-percentage-point credibility interval. The poll shows that 3 percent are unsure or would not vote and 3 percent would pick someone else or another party. The survey of 800 self-identified registered voters, including 660 likely voters, was conducted August 3-12. A poll from the Carolina Journal showed Cooper ahead of Whatley by 12.5 points, 51.5 percent to 39 percent. Other candidates received support from 4.7 percent of respondents, while 4.8 percent were still undecided. The poll surveyed 600 respondents from August 9-10, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. An Elon University poll showed Cooper up 11 points, 53 percent to 42 percent. Three percent of respondents said they would vote for other candidates, while 2 percent were still undecided. Cooper’s lead was bolstered by his support among independents, who broke for him 49 percent to Whatley’s 22 percent, according to the poll. It surveyed 800 North Carolina voters from July 23-31, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 5.6 percentage points. A Fox News poll showed Cooper up 9 points, 53 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 1,005 registered voters from July 23-27. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political Report rates the race as Lean Democratic, writing in an April update, “We’ve long believed the North Carolina Senate race is the GOP seat Democrats are most likely to flip.” Sabato’s Crystal Ball shares the same rating. Texas Senate Race “Texas is a red state, but this cycle, due in large part to the unpopularity of the Trump administration, is a pink state, with its U.S. Senate race landing in the purple category due to Texas Republican primary voters’ decision to nominate the most flawed major statewide candidate in modern GOP history,” Mark Jones, a politics professor at Rice University, recently told Newsweek. Texas has backed Republican presidential nominees in every election since 1980, but Democrats hope 2026 will offer one of their best opportunities in years to compete statewide. Trump carried Texas by 13.7 percentage points in 2024, defeating Harris 56 percent to around 42.5 percent. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped its electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's 2018 Senate bid against Ted Cruz. The GOP's decades-long hold on Texas statewide offices will be tested in November, with the Senate race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Representative James Talarico nearly deadlocked. Surveys show both Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, and Talarico, who has served as a state representative since 2018, holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign. The matchup follows Paxton's defeat of longtime Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary in late May. The race remains highly competitive, with recent polls alternating between narrow Democratic and Republican leads and statistical ties. An Overton Insights/Texas Public Policy Foundation poll of 1,167 likely voters from August 24 to August 26 found Talarico and Paxton locked in a statistical dead heat. The poll found Talarico leading with 44 percent support to Paxton's 43.4 percent, while 12.6 percent of respondents remained undecided. When leaners were included, the race was effectively tied, with both candidates receiving 50 percent support. “This poll fits in with the general trend shown by most other polls that the 2026 statewide elections in Texas are very competitive, with Greg Abbott outperforming Ken Paxton, or Gina Hinojosa underperforming James Talarico,” Jones told Newsweek. Other recent polling, such as an Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters, also puts the Senate race in near deadlock, with 47 percent backing Paxton and 46 percent supporting Talarico. About 5 percent are undecided and 2 percent back a different candidate. The poll was conducted August 9-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Texas voters found that 51 percent back Talarico and 48 percent Paxton, with 1 percent undecided. The survey was conducted July 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as “toss up.” Alaska Trump easily carried Alaska in the 2024 presidential election, winning 54.5 percent of the vote to Harris' 41.4 percent, a margin of about 13.1 percentage points. In 2020, he won by a smaller margin, about 53 percent to Biden’s 43 percent. Despite Alaska's Republican tilt at the presidential level, Democrats have remained competitive in statewide races, aided in part by the state's ranked choice voting system. Alaska Senate Race The Senate contest has emerged as one of Democrats' more plausible pickup opportunities in 2026. Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is seeking another term, while Democrats are backing former Representative Mary Peltola, who won a special House election in 2022 before losing reelection in 2024. Peltola has gained a clearer route to the Senate after fellow Democrat David Leslie withdrew earlier this week, leaving her as the only Democrat against three Republicans in this closely watched midterm race. Voters will now choose among Peltola, Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., and Gerald Heikes on November 3. Polling has been fairly limited, with several small polls and leads within the margin of error. A Data for Progress survey of 605 likely voters in Alaska found that in the first round of voting, no candidate received an outright majority, with 47 percent saying they would vote for Peltola compared to 41 percent for Sullivan. In Alaska, all candidates appear on a single ballot regardless of party, and the four with the most support advance to the general election. Three percent said they would vote for Gerald Heikes, another Republican candidate, while 5 percent were undecided. In the final round of ranked choice voting, however, Peltola led Sullivan by 6 points, 53 percent to 47 percent, according to the poll. It surveyed 605 likely voters in Alaska from July 28 to August 4, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. An Alaska Survey Research poll put Peltola ahead of Sullivan 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent in the final round. It surveyed 1,371 likely voters from August 2-5, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. However, a June New York Times/Siena College poll found Sullivan ahead 47 percent to 45 percent, with about 5 percent undecided. The poll of 593 Alaskan voters was conducted between June 15 and 19 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as a toss-up. Alaska Governor’s Race Democrats are eyeing Alaska's gubernatorial race as a rare opportunity to win the governor's office in a state that has not elected a Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002. However, with former state Senator Tom Begich suspending his campaign Friday night, it remains unclear if Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins can unify Democratic voters and independents to mount a successful campaign against Republican candidates, including Bernadette Wilson and Dave Bronson, who also advanced to the general election after the state’s jungle primary. Kreiss-Tomkins had led the field in the state’s primary with 22.5 percent of the vote, while Begich’s support stood at 20.8 percent. Republican candidates followed behind, with Wilson securing about 10 percent and Bronson about 8 percent. Ranked choice voting is used in the general election. Voters will rank the three candidates by preference. If no candidate receives a majority of support, the candidate with the fewest votes will be eliminated, and their votes will be redistributed according to their second choice. If, after the second round, no candidate receives a majority, the process repeats to declare the winner. Public polling in Alaska's governor's race has been limited, and no publicly available surveys have been released since the primary narrowed the field to four candidates. Before suspending his campaign, Begich had led the Democratic field in several polls and, at times, outpolled Republican candidates. The latest poll from Alaska Survey Research showed Begich leading the pack with 19.7 percent, followed by Wilson with 14.6 percent, Kreiss-Tomkins with 12.2 percent, and Bronson with 10.9 percent. In a third-round ballot test, Begich and Wilson were virtually tied, with Begich receiving 28.7 percent support and Wilson 28.3 percent. Bronson followed at 22.2 percent, while Kreiss-Tomkins received 20.7 percent. The poll surveyed 1,528 registered voters June 30-July 1, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. An earlier Alaska Survey Research poll, which surveyed 1,923 likely voters April 16-19, showed that in the final round of ranked choice, Begich led Wilson 53.9 percent to 46.1 percent. The margin of error was plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. The Cook Political Report rates the race as likely Republican, while Sabato’s Crystal Ball puts it as a toss-up. Ultimately, all of the contests will be decided on November 3, offering one of the clearest tests of the political environment under Trump's second term and the extent to which either party can expand its coalition ahead of the 2028 presidential race. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.

news.title: Stephen A Smith explains why he regrets voting for Harris, says her loyalty to Biden 'usurped everything else'
news.text: ESPN's Stephen A. Smith was repeatedly confronted over why he said he regretted voting for former Vice President Kamala Harris during a podcast released Wednesday, as hosts Cari Champion and Jemele Hill suggested he was targeting Black women. "Flagrant and Funny" hosts Cari Champion and Jemele Hill questioned Smith about his comments that he regretted supporting Harris in 2024, after he said it was the Democrats' plan all along to install her as the replacement for former President Joe Biden in the presidential race. Smith referenced the widely criticized moment from ABC’s ‘The View’ on Oct. 8, 2024, when Harris appeared and said she couldn’t think of anything she’d do differently than Joe Biden. "Because when she went on 'The View' and she sat up there and said she couldn't think of anything that she would do differently, something that Sunny Hostin threw up intentionally as a softball for her to knock out the park. I'm like, when she passed up on that opportunity, this is not a dumb woman. This is a former state attorney general. This is a former senator. This is a former vice president of the United States. She is not dumb. There's only one reason she said that, because her loyalty to Joe Biden usurped everything else," Smith said. HUNTER BIDEN SAYS KAMALA HARRIS IS GETTING 'BAD POLITICAL ADVICE,' REFUSES TO EXPLAIN LOYALTY CRITICISM He added, "And I'm like, 'You trying to win a damn presidency? This is embarrassing. Do you want the presidency or don't you?'" Hill suggested Harris was trying to lean into Biden's accomplishments, and said, "He accomplished a lot." "But I understand when Sunny gave her that easy layup," Champion pressed. "But still, why was it necessary to say that you regretted voting for Kamala Harris when you knew that would take all of the hard work in which she tried to put together away from what she did?" Smith said he supported Harris throughout the election and that he made the comments afterward. STEPHEN A SMITH CALLS TRUMP AN 'UPGRADE' COMPARED TO BIDEN AMID NEW YORK KNICKS FEUD "I get where you're coming from, Cari, I really do. I think that it should have been far more upsetting if it was something that I said before the election. I did not. I supported her leading up to the election. I voted for her. I was on the airwaves talking about what it's going to take to win, win, win. And when it was over, I was honest about how I felt in the moment that that transpired," he said. Champion accused Smith of targeting Black women specifically, and said he could have made his point about his criticisms without saying he regretted voting for Harris. STEPHEN A SMITH GOES OFF ON NATIONAL BLACK JOURNALISTS ORGANIZATION AFTER 'PERSONAL HIT JOB' AGAINST HIM Smith countered, "Can you concede that it's a disagreement as opposed to a disparagement?" She said she couldn't concede the point before the three turned to Smith's dispute with Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas. AMERICA OWES BLACK WOMEN 'EVERYTHING,' REP JASMINE CROCKETT RANTS OVER JULY 4 WEEKEND Harris's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Curtis Houck, the managing editor of the Media Research Center's NewsBusters.org, told Fox News Digital, "This level of refreshing honesty from Stephen A. Smith has sadly been in short supply for far too long. Along with ideological diversity, more commentators and journalists should be willing to admit when they're wrong or express regret. The national media demand the utmost transparency and rigorous reflection from the people they cover, so why not have it go both ways?" Houck continued, "There's a reason why Smith is succeeding by moving outside his normal ideological bubbles. We need more of that from the ruling class, not less." During an April interview with Sage Steele, Smith was asked about his comments prior to the 2024 election on Dave Rubin's show about voting for Harris. "You went on his show, and you said that you voted for Kamala Harris?" Steele asked. "Yes," Smith responded. Steele then added, "And that you regretted it," to which Smith answered, "Yeah." Smith went on to explain that he cast that vote because he believed Harris was capable of compromise, but said he later concluded Democrats still did not understand why they lost. "I also believed that she was the kind of person that… could work across the aisle," Smith said. "And then when I saw how things were unfolding and how out in the clouds the Democratic Party was even after they lost the election, I just said, ‘There’s no hope.’" CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE In January 2025, Smith said during an interview with Bill Maher, "Yes, I voted for her, a lot of people voted for her, but in the end, we end up feeling like d--- fools, because we supported it. We fell for the okiedoke as they say. If you had a primary, the likelihood is she would not have been the Democratic nominee." news.summary: Stephen A. Smith defended his Kamala Harris vote regret on Cari Champion and Jemele Hill's podcast as the hosts accused him of targeting Black women.

news.title: Some battleground Republicans set to skip GOP midterm convention next week
news.text:
Ahead of next week's Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, which is set to tout President Donald Trump's record at a time when he still faces low approval ratings and a negative political environment, several battleground Republicans told ABC News that they either aren't going to the convention or are still undecided.

Next week, the Republican Party will hold its first-ever midterm convention in an effort to sell its message to voters before the high-stakes midterm elections in November.

Republican Rep. Zach Nunn of Iowa, running in one of the top House districts that Democrats hope to flip this cycle, told ABC News that he will be in his district while the convention is occurring.

"We're going to be back in our district working hard," Nunn said of Iowa's 3rd Congressional District.

Arizona Rep. Juan Ciscomani told ABC News that he will not attend the convention because he has his debate for the state's 6th Congressional District is on Sept. 10, the second night of the convention.

"It's a televised, pre-scheduled debate. We can't move it," Ciscomani said.

Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, running to defend his seat in Pennsylvania's 7th Congressional District, said he's still undecided about whether or not he will attend next week's convention, saying it will depend on his schedule.

Asked what the hesitation is with attending the convention, Mackenzie said, "We need to know what's going on at the convention, and we're still waiting to see all the different scheduling items there."

Asked if he thinks it would be better for his reelection bid to be back in his district rather than at the convention, Mackenzie said he'll take a better look at attending the convention once more details fall into place.

"I think we spend all of our time at home as much as possible, and obviously there are political events and activities that come up as well. So, we'll take a look once we have all the people," Mackenzie said.

Even Rep. Lauren Boebert, who is running for reelection in her solidly red Colorado district, is undecided on whether she'll attend the convention next week.

"We'll see," said Boebert, who has criticized Trump, when asked by reporters Wednesday afternoon.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the only Republican senator to win in a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in the 2024 election, will also not be attending next week's midterm convention. Collins has long avoided political conventions during election cycles.

The lawmakers' decisions come as a Reuters/Ipsos poll released earlier this week found Trump's approval rating remains at the lowest of either of his two terms, at 33%. Trump is set to attend the convention as well as deliver a keynote address.

Despite several battleground Republicans not attending next week's convention, roughly 100 House Republican members and candidates are expected to be in Dallas; that is still about half of the House GOP and candidates running this fall for reelection.

The House Republican campaign committee is also asking lawmakers and candidates to contribute between $25,000 and $100,000 to the House Republican campaign committee if they plan to attend, multiple Republicans briefed on the request told ABC News.

GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden, who is running for reelection in Wisconsin's competitive 3rd Congressional District, is one of the House members who will attend next week's convention, writing on X that the event will be an amazing platform to discuss Republicans' wins over the past year and a half.

Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Ohio Senate candidate Sen. Jon Husted will both attend next week's convention, according to their campaigns.

Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Scott Perry is also planning to attend, according to a campaign spokesperson; his district -- the state's 10th Congressional District -- is one of four that Democrats are targeting in Pennsylvania.

Even candidates in some of the most critical gubernatorial races are missing next week's convention to campaign in their respective states, candidates said.

Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson, who is running against Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, will not be attending the convention, his campaign said.

Wisconsin GOP gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany also will not attend. Tiffany’s campaign told ABC News it has campaign events scheduled in different parts of the state on Sept. 9 and 10.

ABC News' Oren Oppenheim and Gaby Vinick contributed to this report.
news.summary: Several battleground Republicans told ABC News they either weren't going to the convention or were still undecided.
news.author: Benjamin Siegel,Hannah Demissie

news.title: State probes funds, freezes some payments at Arab American business group
news.text:
State agencies have launched investigations into alleged embezzlement and frozen some payment activity at the largest Arab American business group in Michigan, which recently fired its executive director.

Last month, on Aug. 21, the Dearborn-based American Arab Chamber of Commerce announced it terminated Bilal Hammoud, its executive director since February 2024, saying that some "funds could not be accounted for." Now, state agencies tell the Detroit Free Press they have launched investigations and reviews of some state funding for the chamber and its business incubator, Tejara, which in recent years has received millions of dollars in state money.

Hammoud was described as Tejara's CEO in a news release from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in May 2025, when she appointed Hammoud to the Michigan Workforce Development Board. The chamber and Tejara share a similar address, but are listed as separate groups on their Form 990s, tax records show.

"I can confirm the Michigan Department of Attorney General is investigating the matter regarding alleged embezzlement from the American Arab Chamber of Commerce," Danny Wimmer, press secretary for state Attorney General Dana Nessel, told the Free Press. Wimmer did not say how long the investigation will take place or whether any charges may stem from it.

Other state agencies are helping with the investigation. The Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC) said it's "collaborating with both the State Budget Office and the Department of Attorney General in investigating this alleged embezzlement," Danielle Emerson, public relations manager for the MEDC, told the Free Press. "This particular grant program model and processes were reviewed and approved by third parties (Accenture and Guidehouse), and we are reviewing those processes in real time."

After learning about the allegations on Aug. 21, "we immediately froze all payment activity related to the open grant with Tejara and began gathering facts," Emerson said. Three days later, on Aug. 24, "we reached out to the Attorney General’s office to establish an open line of communication to coordinate on any prospective AG investigation."

Emerson of MEDC explained how the grant money was given to Tejara.

"MEDC authorized payments to the correct grant recipient," she said. "Those authorized payments were then disbursed through the state’s SIGMA (Statewide Integrated Governmental Management Application) system to the bank account identified within the grant recipient’s SIGMA profile. Information in those grant recipient profiles is controlled by the customer. MEDC does not have access or control over customer SIGMA accounts."

$3.4 million awarded to Dearborn business group

The MEDC awarded the Chamber's Tejara program $3.43 million in 2023 as part of a statewide effort to support entrepreneurial hubs.

"All $3.4 million was distributed to the Arab American Chamber of Commerce, as all relevant milestones were met and sufficient qualified expenditures were demonstrated," Emerson said. "The initial disbursement of about $1.7 million (50% of the grant) was made in March 2024. Successive payments of about $856,000 (25% of the grant) were made in January and July 2026."

MEDC also gave money several years ago to Tejara or the American Arab Chamber of Commerce for "an MEDC sponsorship of an event," Emerson said.

The firing of Hammoud and the investigation come after another case involving alleged improprieties with a former executive director at the American Arab Chamber of Commerce, Fay Beydoun, who worked at the chamber before Hammoud. Beydoun was charged by Nessel in May with 16 criminal counts, including conducting a criminal enterprise, tied to a $20 million grant she received from the state administered through the MEDC for a nonprofit she formed, Global Link International, that was separate from the chamber. In June 2025, Nessel's office raided the MEDC office in connection with their Beydoun investigation.

Arab American advocates in metro Detroit have expressed concern about the cases, saying it could harm the reputation of community groups.

"The damage extends beyond the Chamber," attorney James Allen, a former chairman of the American Arab Chamber of Commerce, said in an article in the Arab American News. "Arab American organizations spent generations building credibility in Metropolitan Detroit and throughout Michigan, demonstrating that our community could responsibly steward public and private resources. That reputation is an asset, and it can be squandered."

Hammoud has been active within the Democratic Party and community groups, running in 2022 in the primary for a state House seat that he lost to State Rep. Erin Byrnes. He also once served as Public Engagement Associate in the executive office of Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, working to support Arabic-language ballots in Dearborn, and is on the boards of several groups. In 2024, Hammoud and other Arab American leaders met with Secretary of State Antony Blinken to express their concerns about Israel's attacks in Gaza. In Feb. 2025, Hammoud and others traveled with Whitmer to the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain on an investment mission.

Hammoud's attorney, Ray Cassar, said in a statement that Hammoud is cooperating with investigators.

"It is early on in the investigation, but I can tell you that Bilal is a good young man who is deeply sorry for the negative publicity that he has caused," Cassar said. "Both the American Arab Chamber of Commerce and Tejara are great organizations that serve the community in many ways. He has cooperated with the internal investigation and will continue to do so."

State Budget Office has 'zero tolerance' for fraud

The State Budget Office is also reviewing the funds given to the chamber, saying it has deactivated an account tied to the Tejara grant.

"The State of Michigan has a zero-tolerance policy for fraud or misuse of taxpayer dollars," Cole Pachucki, a spokesman for the State Budget Office, told the Detroit Free Press. "Upon learning of allegations that an individual associated with the grant recipient may have improperly redirected grant funds, SBO (State Budget Office) quickly deactivated the account at issue to prevent any further activity. A thorough grant review was swiftly launched to determine what may have occurred and strengthen oversight, controls, and safeguards to help prevent similar issues from occurring in the future."

The State Budget Office is "prepared to fully cooperate with any criminal investigation, and will take appropriate action to hold accountable any individual found to have improperly used or redirected grant funds and pursue the recovery of any taxpayer dollars found to have been misused," Pachucki said.

More: Dearborn lawyer who won primary accused of ethics violations by state

Tejara received a total of $1.7 million in payments in January and July, out of the $3.4 million awarded in 2023, and also received $217,000 in 2025 through a second grant administered by the Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity, Pachucki added. State officials did not say how much Hammoud may have embezzled; a report by WXYZ-TV, citing unnamed sources, says Hammoud is accused of misappropriating more than $1 million.

“The moment we recognized there was a problem, we acted to protect this institution and the people who depend on it,” Ahmad Chebbani, a cofounder and chairman of the chamber's board, said in a statement to the Free Press provided by publicist Chris Moyer.

Chebbani said he met with members of the state's attorney general's office on Aug. 25 "because we are committed to full cooperation and to being accountable to everyone who places their trust in this chamber.”

In addition, the chamber hired "Warner Norcross + Judd to lead an independent investigation, and referred the matter to the Dearborn Police Department and the Michigan Attorney General’s office," the statement from Moyer read.

Founded in 1992, the American Arab Chamber of Commerce drew national attention in 2003 for holding a U.S.-Arab Economic Forum in Detroit at a time of tensions in the Middle East after the U.S. invaded Iraq. Sec. of State Colin Powell delivered a speech at the event, which sought to improve business ties between the U.S. and the Arab world. The chamber formed Tejara as a "strategic initiative" that is an "innovation and entrepreneurship hub elevating underrepresented and immigrant founders into tomorrow’s leading companies across North America and beyond," the chamber's website says.

In October 2024, the chamber's cofounder and chairman, Ahmad Chebbani, endorsed Kamala Harris for president, drawing criticism from Arab Americans upset over U.S. support for Israeli attacks in Gaza and Lebanon. A few days after his endorsement, the chamber hosted a State Department official at its annual gala dinner.

Contact Niraj Warikoo: nwarikoo@freepress.com

news.title: Dem Senate nominee changes tune on ICE after vowing not 'one more dime' for agency
news.text: A Democrat running for the Senate in ruby-red Arkansas once called to defund immigration enforcement, but has since changed her tune. Arkansas Senate Democratic nominee Hallie Shoffner, a farmer and political newcomer whose first time in the political arena is this midterm cycle, is running to unseat Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., in November. As Election Day creeps closer, Cotton has gone on the offensive against her, attacking an apparent flip-flop in her position on Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the immigration enforcement agency under the Department of Homeland Security that became a political lightning rod in Congress earlier this year. DEM REP SETH MOULTON SAYS PARTY HAS NO IMMIGRATION PLAN, IS ONLY ‘OPPOSITION TO TRUMP’ Shoffner, during an appearance in June at the Immigrant Heritage Month Business Expo in Springdale, Ark., was asked whether she would defund ICE — a position several Democrats running for office have taken this cycle, including progressives Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota. "I would vote to defund ICE as it exists right now," Shoffner said. "Immigration and Customs Enforcement was created not that long ago, and it no longer serves the purpose it was originally created for." "I would not spend one more dime on ICE, because — not just because of the human dignity issue — but also the fact that it is now the largest law enforcement agency in the country," she continued. "It has 10 times the budget of the organization that fights child sex trafficking." GOP ADVANCES ICE FUNDING PACKAGE AFTER FORCING TRUMP'S CONTROVERSIAL $2B FUND INTO RETREAT ICE became a political third rail earlier this year after fatal shootings in Minnesota and was at the center of the longest government shutdown in history, when Senate Democrats refused to fund the agency absent stringent reforms. That prompted Senate Republicans to front-load $70 billion in funding for ICE and Border Patrol earlier this year. Cotton’s campaign cut Shoffner's comments into attack ads and accused her of donating to former Vice President Kamala Harris 25 times, which prompted Shoffner to further define her position. In a Facebook post from Tuesday in which Cotton was asked by a voter about Shoffner’s ICE position, she jumped into the comment section to argue, "I don’t want to defund ICE, I want to reform it." ‘ABOLISH ICE’ DEMOCRAT FREEZES IN LIVE INTERVIEW WHEN ASKED WHO SHOULD ENFORCE IMMIGRATION LAWS "My opponent wants to defund ICE, just like Democrat socialists Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez and Abdul El-Sayed," Cotton told Fox News Digital. "Doing so would protect criminals from deportation, like the illegal alien gang member who was arrested in Carroll County just days ago. Defunding ICE would make Arkansas more dangerous." Shoffner’s bid to unseat Cotton, who is running for a third term in the upper chamber, is one of the tougher battles during this midterm cycle for Democrats. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Arkansas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since former Sen. Mark Pryor, who Cotton defeated in 2014. Shoffner also doesn’t have the backing of the Democratic establishment, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., in Washington, D.C. Shoffner has put distance between herself and Schumer, too, telling Politico in March that while Democrats had found the issue of affordability to be a "magic bullet" at the national level, Arkansans were going to give Schumer "the side eye, because what does he know about affordability?"
news.summary: Hallie Shoffner said she'd defund ICE at an Arkansas event, but Tom Cotton's attack ads prompted her to redefine her immigration enforcement stance.

news.title: Chris Pappas Faces Second Polling Blow in New Hampshire Race Against Sununu
news.text: Democratic Representative Chris Pappas was dealt a second polling blow against former Senator John Sununu, a Republican, in New Hampshire’s U.S. Senate race, a must-win for Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections. Pappas and Sununu are viewed as front-runners to win their party’s nominations next week in the race to succeed retiring Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen in November. Republicans see the race in the Granite State, which backed Vice President Kamala Harris by about 3 points in 2024, as a potential pickup opportunity due to the candidacy of Sununu, who held the seat from 2003 to 2009. But Democrats believe Pappas, who represents a swing district, should be well-positioned to win, particularly in a national environment fueled by voter frustration with President Donald Trump. However, two recent polls showed Sununu with a slight lead over Pappas. Forecasters still view Democrats as having a slight edge, but the polling presents a new warning sign for Democrats as they work against a challenging map to win a Senate majority in November. Pappas’ campaign manager, Rachel Petri, wrote in a statement to Newsweek that voters “know the difference between a candidate who hides and one who fights.” “Trump’s handpicked candidate John Sununu can hide in his basement and let outside groups spend millions of dollars trying to buy him this election, but Chris Pappas is going to keep doing what he’s done from day one: show up, talk to voters, and earn their support the New Hampshire way,” Petri wrote. Newsweek also reached out to the Sununu campaign for comment via email. John Sununu Leads Chris Pappas in Two Latest Polls The latest poll from GOP pollster Fabrizio, Lee & Associates showed the race in a statistical tie, with Sununu receiving 37 percent support and Pappas 36 percent. Other candidates received less than 4 percent support, while 23 percent were undecided about who they would vote for. The pollster surveyed 600 likely voters in New Hampshire from August 27-30, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. It comes just days after a University of New Hampshire poll similarly showed Sununu with a lead, 45 percent to 43 percent. At the same time, Pappas led former Massachusetts Senator Scott Brown, who is also running in the GOP primary, by 5 points, 45 percent to 40 percent. It surveyed 1,878 likely voters August 20-24 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.3 percentage points. Brown represented Massachusetts in the Senate from 2010 to 2013 but lost reelection to Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren in the solidly blue state. Pappas has represented New Hampshire’s 1st District in Congress since 2019. Sununu served as a senator in the 2000s and is part of a prominent political family in New Hampshire. His father, John Sununu, and brother, Chris Sununu, have served as the state’s governor. Chris Pappas Led Earlier Polls Earlier polling of the race showed Pappas leading Sununu in the single digits. For example, a Saint Anselm College poll, conducted among 1,411 likely voters August 17-18, showed Pappas up 7 points on Sununu, 48 percent to 41 percent, and 12 points over Brown, 49 percent to 37 percent. A Peak Insights poll, a GOP internal, showed Pappas up a point, 43 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 500 respondents June 24-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Earlier UNH polls also showed Pappas leading. In June, the pollster showed him up 3 points over Sununu, 47 percent to 44 percent. He led by 7 points, 49 percent to 42 percent, in April, and 5 points, 50 percent to 45 percent, in January, according to the pollster. Pappas and Sununu are focusing on issues of affordability and the cost of living. Pappas has emphasized healthcare and pledged to tackle corruption. Sununu has also been emphasizing affordability on the campaign trail and has been more critical of the war in Iran than Brown. When Is New Hampshire Primary? The New Hampshire primary is set for September 8. Sununu is facing Brown but has held a strong lead in polls. He has consolidated support from the GOP and has received Trump's endorsement. Pappas, who is running against scientist Karishma Manzur, a progressive, has also led in primary polling. The latest UNH poll showed him up 13 points, 47 percent to 34 percent, a narrower margin than other surveys. A GQR poll, a Pappas internal that surveyed 422 likely voters August 19-25, showed him up by a larger margin, 71 percent to 15 percent. What Do Prediction Markets Say? Prediction markets continue to give Democrats a strong advantage in the New Hampshire Senate race. As of Thursday, Democrats had an 83 percent chance of victory on Kalshi and an 84 percent chance on Polymarket, an indication that traders have not been swayed by a few close polls. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment in the moment but do not always predict the future accurately. GOP Victory in New Hampshire Would Complicate Dems’ Senate Math Democrats are already facing a difficult Senate map with limited obvious pickup opportunities despite the favorable national environment, and Republicans pulling off an upset victory in New Hampshire would make the task even more difficult. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, so Democrats have to pick up four seats in November to win a majority, as Vice President JD Vance is the tiebreaker for Republicans. In addition to New Hampshire, Democrats are defending two seats in swing states won by Trump in 2024—Georgia and Michigan. They view GOP-held seats in Maine, which Trump lost by 7 points, and North Carolina, which he carried by 3 points, as top pick-up opportunities. But there are no other seats up for grabs in states where Trump either won by single digits or lost in 2024, so Democrats have to win in more conservative places like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas to stand a chance of flipping the Senate. If they win all of the more competitive races, they would have to flip two of those seats. If New Hampshire flips to the GOP, they would have to win three to win a majority, a difficult but not impossible task. New Hampshire: GOP’s Elusive Swing State At the federal level, New Hampshire has emerged as an elusive state for Republicans. Although it regularly backs Republican governors, it has continued to lean Democratic in federal races. It last voted for a Republican president in 2000. In the Trump era, Democrats have run strong in Senate races, winning each since 2016. The state is viewed as competitive for both parties but is generally seen as politically moderate with a libertarian streak, and it has backed politicians from both parties over the years. In 2024, the state narrowly went to Harris, 50.7 percent to 47.9 percent. But it gave President Joe Biden a wider victory in 2020, backing him by 7 points. In 2016, it was one of the country's closest races, backing former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by less than half a percentage point. New Hampshire’s southern and central region is fairly dense around cities like Manchester, Concord, Portsmouth, Dover and Nashua. Many of those cities are more Democratic, though not always overwhelmingly. Manchester, for instance, backed Harris by less than 8 points in 2024. But many of the suburbs and smaller towns in southern New Hampshire are more Republican. College towns like Durham and Keene are also critical for Democrats. The northern part is more rural. Areas in the White Mountains that depend on tourism lean Democratic, though some other sparsely populated areas are more conservative. Independent voters are key in the state. As of August 3, 351,815 New Hampshirites were not registered with either party, according to the secretary of state’s office. There were 299,976 registered Republicans and 247,069 registered Democrats. Winning the independent voters will be key for either candidate in November. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Trump never won New Hampshire in his presidential runs, but Republicans see it as a pickup opportunity in this year's midterms.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: At the Races: Labor Day reds and blues
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the CQ Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Daniela Altimari, Mary Ellen McIntire and Niels Lesniewski

Organized labor is ramping up for the midterms.

In her annual State of the Unions address this week, AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler laid out the labor federation’s concerns and how it intends to mobilize its members.

Affordability, including the cost of housing and health care, along with the social and economic upheaval presented by AI, are among the chief worries of the AFL-CIO’s nearly 15 million members.

“It's harder to win on AI when we have politicians, Republicans and Democrats alike, who cash checks from Big Tech CEOs instead of doing their job and regulating them,’’ Shuler said. “That's why these midterm elections matter. If we don't right the ship in November, it gets that much harder to build an economy that works for all of us.”

Donald Trump made historic gains with working-class voters in 2024; Teamsters President Sean O’Brien even had a speaking role at the Republican National Convention. Teamster branches have endorsed an array of Republican candidates this cycle, including in Kansas, where Teamsters Local 696 in Topeka announced Thursday it was backing Sen. Roger Marshall for reelection.

But since returning to the White House the Trump administration has tangled with unions representing federal workers and sought to make it harder for labor to organize.

Still, Shuler cautioned that Democrats shouldn’t take union workers for granted. 

“Workers are sick and tired of both parties. Republicans … enable a White House that has made our life worse and more expensive at every turn … have rubber-stamped Trump's needless wars, chaotic tariffs, and attacks on our communities,” she said. “ At the same time, we have too many Democrats who pay lip service to working people, say they understand us and want our votes on Election Day, and then take office and cozy up to the same corporations we're fighting on the picket lines.”

The union is launching its largest effort ever to mobilize for the midterms: Through door-knocking, get-out-the vote initiatives and regular conversations with co-workers and family members, the AFL-CIO aims to turn out 16 million voters, 2 million more than it says it brought out in 2022.

The group has endorsed candidates for House, Senate and governor’s races across the spectrum, from democratic socialists and moderate Democrats to independents and one Republican seeking federal office: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

The fifth-term congressman who represents a Philadelphia-area swing district called the endorsement “a proud honor.”

Starting gate

#NH01: The tenor of the Democratic primary for the seat New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas is vacating for his Senate run has turned increasingly sour ahead of Tuesday’s election, with both front-runners, Maura Sullivan and Stefany Shaheen, taking swipes at each other. Recent polls show Sullivan pulling ahead of Shaheen, but many voters remained undecided. 

Mass. message: The results of Tuesday’s Democratic primaries in Massachusetts were a mixed bag, with signs for optimism for candidates across the generational and ideological spectrum. Sen. Edward J. Markey, an 80-year-old progressive who’s been in Congress for nearly five decades, won his primary. So did two septuagenarian House Democrats, Reps. Richard E. Neal and Stephen F. Lynch, who turned back younger, more liberal challengers by highlighting the benefits of seniority and their skill at bringing federal funding home to their districts. And an establishment-linked candidate, Dan Koh, won the Democratic primary for an open House seat, bolstered by endorsements from former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Bad bet: Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel running against Democratic Rep. Don Davis in a key North Carolina swing district, was fined and suspended by the prediction market Kalshi after she bet on her campaign. The platform also announced it was penalizing several other former candidates for violating its rules, including disgraced GOP former Rep. George Santos of New York, who drew a lifetime ban. 

State of emergency: Some Democrats and voting rights advocates are taking seriously the possibility that Trump could declare a national emergency before the midterms if the Senate does not pass the GOP-crafted elections package, known as the SAVE America Act, our colleague John T. Bennett writes.

Trump on the road: The president told vulnerable Republican candidates he plans to hit the campaign trail hard starting 30 days out from Election Day, Bennett reports. “We're going to do something like I did for myself in the last presidential election,” Trump said at a Rose Garden dinner Wednesday. “I'm not going to go out and play golf. I'm not going to do anything. All I'm going to do is work, work, work and fight, fight, fight and win, win, win.” His announcement comes as The Washington Post reports that Republicans are concerned it may be too late to fully deploy the millions of dollars in Trump’s super PAC to support GOP candidates this fall. 

Speaker on the road: Speaker Mike Johnson hit the campaign trail in 54 cities and towns over 18 states during the August recess on behalf of 71 members and candidates, the Louisiana Republican announced this week. 

Texas money: Senate Majority Leader John Thune is encouraging Trump and his aligned group MAGA Inc. to spend in Texas, where GOP nominee Ken Paxton is facing a tough race against Democrat James Talarico. The South Dakota Republican's appeal comes after The Texas Tribune reported last week that Sen. John Cornyn, whom Paxton defeated in the primary, has been fundraising for GOP Senate candidates in several states, but not Texas. 

#MISEN: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, apologized for a comment he made in March about an attack on a synagogue near Detroit, telling members of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus that he made a “mistake,” when he said “hurt people hurt people” after a man drove a truck into a synagogue. Some Jewish Democrats have been skeptical of El-Sayed’s candidacy in the key swing state.

Country roads, take him home? Politico reports that freshman Sen. Jim Justice of West Virginia is pondering a return to the governor’s office. The Republican is considering launching a primary challenge to Gov. Patrick Morrisey, with whom he’s been feuding in recent days. 

A family affair: A new ad for GOP Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr.’s reelection campaign features his 91-year-old namesake father, a popular former Garden State governor, who says the 7th District congressman “worked to protect Medicare and Medicaid for every New Jersey senior, child, disabled person.” Kean is in a tight reelection fight with Democratic Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett. 

#GirlDad: Candidate ads featuring daughters were a micro-trend in 2024 and the theme appears to be making a comeback this year. A new ad by Ohio Democrat Brian Poindexter features his three daughters talking about his work ethic, while Nebraska Republican Brinker Harding spotlights his wife and two daughters in his ad.

Last Frontier funny business: The fall lineups are set in Alaska but only after a cascade of candidate withdrawals before the Monday deadline to finalize the top four November ballot. The Senate contest pits Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola against two Dan Sullivans, including the incumbent GOP senator, and another Republican. In the House race, GOP Rep. Nick Begich will take on independent Bill Hill, who is backed by Democrats, Democrat Eric Hafner, who currently resides in a federal prison in New York, and Libertarian Jim McDermott, who finished eighth but moved up after other candidates withdrew. And in the governor’s race, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins will be the only Democrat on the ballot after Tom Begich (uncle to the current congressman) dropped out. Republicans took the other three spots, but not before a last-minute shakeup that landed a disqualified candidate’s wife on the ballot. 

Guv roundup: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, who ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination Tuesday, will face Republican former medical tech executive Mike Minogue in her bid for a second term. In Florida, outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis finally endorsed GOP Rep. Byron Donalds’ campaign for governor. Donalds, who faces Democrat David Jolly in November, picked state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate last week. And in Nebraska, former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom, whose independent gubernatorial bid fell through this summer, has filed to challenge GOP Gov. Jim Pillen under the America First Party banner. Lindstrom lost to Pillen in the 2022 Republican primary.

Nathan's notes

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections sees potential parallels between this year’s elections and the 2006 midterms, when Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress.

Thanks to mid-decade redistricting, some shuffling is expected to come out of this year's midterm elections.

news.text:
MS NOW’s State of Play

September 3, 2026

11:15:14 AM Eastern

PETER ALEXANDER: We have talked about her impact from the boardroom to the bedroom to the halls of the Capitol. As you say, in 2024, a record 152 women lawmakers were elected. We had never seen ranks of women serving this country like we have seen in recent years. 

You and Miss Steinem fought through three Republican presidencies to advance not just women's rights, but equal rights for everyone. Do you remember some of the advice she gave you when the days seemed dark or more challenging for the movement?

REP. NANCY PELOSI (D-CA): Well, long before I was elected to public office, when I was party chair in California, she said, “We've got to get you doing more things than just politics. We want you to be more active in terms of the women's movement.” And I said, “Well, that's what I think I'm doing.” But then she was unhappy because Time magazine had not put me as the first woman speaker on the cover. And so she had me on the cover of Ms. Magazine. 

So, she was saying, I'm going to make sure that people understand the connection between what I'm doing and what you are doing. But she was - the advice she gave me is what she gave everyone else. Be confident, have courage. Get out there and do make sure you make your difference. And she was a model for that herself. To see the courage she had and the upbringing she had, she overcame it with pride. She was beautiful. She was graceful. She was eloquent. She was effective. And she was a model for the rest of us to be ourselves, know our power, and get the job done.

ALEXANDER: For all the progress that we have seen over the course of your and her lifetime, obviously the last several years have been so challenging. The overturning of Roe v. Wade. As you witness America, as we see it today, the impact that some of the new efforts under this president are having on women - not just women, but certainly women in America. 

Are you troubled? Do you remain optimistic?

PELOSI: Well, I saw the interview with Senator Clinton - I mean, senator - secretary, so many titles for Hillary Clinton this morning. Yes, both optimistic, hopeful, and concerned. 

And I do think that young people, the more they know about what a difference Gloria Steinem made, it's time to refresh the memory of all of us - so many of us, about the challenge that was women were facing and what we have now. 

But we need more. I'm relentless, as Gloria would want us all to be in our pursuit of many more rights for women, many more opportunities for women, and to teach men - Some men need to be taught, really, that respect for women is something that is a tradition in our country that must be honored as we go forward. And a little bit in doubt right now. But we don't agonize about them. We organize about the women.

11:55:46 AM Eastern

ALEXANDER: Gloria Steinem was a supporter of yours. She donated to your campaign in 2020. She participated in your campaign two years ago. When she was asked if a woman could win the presidency, she said, “I think Kamala Harris could win.” What was some of the best advice she gave you through the course of your public life?

FORMER VICE PRESIDENT KAMALA HARRIS: Well, she, you know, and remember, I wasn't the first. She has supported women in the run for the presidency as early as her incredible support for Shirley Chisholm, who is a role model for me, and of course, Hillary Clinton. And her point was always, listen, we have to understand our ability to be, even though people may not see it at the moment, that there is still work to be done to help people with their perception of who can do what. 

But, you know, here's my feeling about it is that, you know, breaking barriers involves breaking. And here's the thing about breaking things. Sometimes you get cut, sometimes you bleed, but it'll be worth it every time. And Gloria knew that. She understood that the process of breaking barriers will be important. It will be historic, but it will also involve pain, and there will be a lot of support for you through that process. Understanding it won't be easy, but it's important to get it done.

ALEXANDER: Madam Vice President, we appreciate all your reflections. I do want to ask you, or give you a chance to respond to one of the headlines that's in the news today. Politico reports that you are wading into some of the midterms and that red-state, not blue or purple state, but red-state Democrats in states that Donald Trump won are encouraging you to stay away for fear it could impact their races there. Your response to some of that reporting?

HARRIS: Listen, Peter, we need to win, okay. Bottom line, we need to win. I have run locally. I've run for statewide office and obviously nationally. And these candidates know what they need to do to win and I would expect nothing less. 

I look forward to being on the trail and helping folks where I can be helpful, but we have got to put a check on this lawless administration and deliver what Americans need and deserve: lower costs, affordable health care, affordable child care, you name it. So, I support them in doing whatever they need to do to win.

ALEXANDER: Are you going to be on the trail for yourself as a presidential candidate in 2028?

HARRIS: I'm focused on ‘26. You know what, Peter? And to be very serious about this: ‘28 doesn't matter if we don't win ‘26 

ALEXANDER: Got it. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Madam Vice President, it's always a pleasure to have you here. Thanks for spending time with us and sharing your reflections about the life of a one-of-a-kind woman, Gloria Steinem. We appreciate you.

HARRIS: Good to be with you. Thank you. Bye.

news.title: The chilling sentence that could stop JD Vance becoming president
news.text:
Vice President JD Vance has made faith a huge part of his political identity.

He wasn’t baptised, but as a teenager attended Pentecostal services after reconnecting with his biological father, who had become devout in the faith. After a phase as an “angry atheist” when he attended Yale Law School, Vance reconnected with religion and eventually, as an adult, converted to Catholicism.

The Vice President seems to take an esoteric approach to his new faith. Earlier this year, Vance said it was “very, very important for the Pope to be careful when he talks about matters of theology” – a bizarre stance for a Catholic convert to take, given that regarding the Pope as the supreme authority on religious matters is very much a requirement of the religion.

This week, Vance has once again brought the spotlight on to his religious beliefs after giving an extended interview to an evangelical podcast. At one stage, he was asked by the host if he’d ever been in a room that was “spiritually dark”, where “you feel like Satan is presently here or there’s blatant evil” around.

Vance confirmed he had, “in meetings with world leaders”, where he would “feel a certain darkness about it” – a unique form of diplomacy for a politician currently charged with trying to negotiate a peace deal with the new leaders of Iran, for example.

But it is Vance’s comments about the Antichrist that have garnered the most attention. Vance insisted that he is “doing as much of God’s work as possible… and that if that leads to the end times, okay”, adding that he would be “not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us”.

A fixation that we might be thousands of years or no more than “a few months” from the Biblical end times – and on wondering who might be the literal Antichrist – is something more suited to the Pentecostal faith of Vance’s youth, rather than the Catholicism he discovered as an adult, and recently published a book about.

Tech mogul Peter Thiel, who previously employed Vance as a venture capitalist, and who then funded his initial run for Senate, is known for his public obsession with the Antichrist – having even suggested it might have taken the form of Swedish eco-activist Greta Thunberg. Similarly, many of the Republican primary voters Vance will need to court for the 2028 presidential nomination are focused on the politics of the end times.

White evangelical Protestants are Maga’s most loyal foot soldiers, and so securing their support is vital to whoever would look to take on his mantle in 2028. Only 23 per cent of US adults are evangelical Protestants, but they make up 31 per cent of the Republicans who still view Donald Trump favourably in 2026. They also broke for Republicans in huge numbers: in 2024, 85 per cent of white evangelical Protestants voted for Trump over Kamala Harris.

More mainstream Christians lean right, but not nearly so hard: 59 per cent of white Catholics voted Trump, as did 57 per cent of mainstream Protestants (by contrast, 83 per cent of Black Protestants voted Harris). It seems Vance has decided his political future lies with the evangelicals – but he might not be going about things in quite the right way. Many Americans will look at Vance’s religiosity with bafflement, if not alarm.Say what you want about Trump – a president not exactly known for his life-long religious devotion, nor for his moral rectitude – but one thing he has been mostly successful at is toeing the line with his religious supporters. Evangelical Maga voters were well aware that Trump was not one of them when they voted for him: his trick was convincing them that despite that, he’s got their best interest at heart, as well as Americans of other faiths.

Crucially, he’s delivered on at least a few of their priorities. It was thanks to Trump’s appointments, after all, that the Supreme Court overturned the decades-old Roe v Wade ruling, which guaranteed abortion rights across the USA – something the Christian right had pursued for decades.

Vance isn’t copying the playbook that has worked so well for his current boss. He seems determined to convince the evangelicals that he’s one of them – belief in the Antichrist and satanic influence, and all. It’s a risky change of tactic, and one that might leave him wishing he’d stuck to Trump’s approach.

news.title: Democrats want amnesia on inflation
news.text:
There’s a reason Democrats are focused on affordability: It is a daily reality, and many Democratic policies make it worse.

Democrats have been running on “affordability” since Joe Biden left office and broke the party’s direct political connection to the inflation surge of his presidency.

Yes, affordability is a problem. But you do not solve a problem by putting the people who helped cause it in charge of fixing it.

When Biden took office in January 2021, inflation was 1.4%. By March, it was 2.6%, and by December, it hit 7%. It reached 7.5% in January 2022, topped 8% in March, and hit 9.1% in June — a 40-year high. By December 2022, it was still 6.5%.

Inflation did not fall below 3% until the latter half of 2024, and it never returned to within one percentage point of the rate Biden inherited.

Democrats spent much of the Biden years defending the administration’s economic record. Now they talk constantly about affordability, even though today’s price level still reflects the inflation Americans absorbed during those years.

That distinction is vital. Slower inflation means prices are rising more slowly; it does not reverse increases already built into the economy. Those higher prices remain unless incomes eventually catch up or prices actually fall.

Politically, that creates an opening. Democrats can campaign against high prices after presiding over the period when those prices rose fastest, while hoping voters forget how they got there. Much of the coverage treats affordability as a fresh problem rather than the cumulative result of years of price increases.

Affordability is national, but it is not uniform. Some states are much more expensive than others, and the partisan pattern is difficult to ignore.

RELATED: Trump’s next tax cut should make Americans owners

 Jim WATSON/AFP/Getty Images

According to World Population Review’s 2026 Cost of Living Index by State, blue states dominate the least-affordable end of the rankings.

Hawaii ranks as the nation’s most expensive state. It voted for Kamala Harris 60.6% to 37.5% in 2024 and has had Democratic trifectas in state government for 27 straight years.

The pattern extends beyond Hawaii. Of the 10 least-affordable states, only Alaska voted Republican in the 2024 presidential election. The next Republican-voting state is Arizona at No. 15. Thirteen of the 15 least-affordable states, and 15 of the top 17, voted Democratic in 2024.

At the other end, Oklahoma is the nation’s most affordable state. It voted for Trump 66.2% to 31.9% in 2024 and has had 16 straight years of Republican trifectas in state government. All 10 of the most affordable states voted Republican in 2024.

Partisanship is not the only thing that determines a state’s cost of living. Geography, housing supply, energy, taxes, regulation, and labor costs all play roles. But policy affects several of those variables directly.

Democratic policies often push costs upward through heavier regulation, higher minimum wages, greater public spending, and higher taxes. Businesses pass many of those costs along. Residents pay the rest directly. Either way, affordability suffers.

That is the bind for Democrats. They see a powerful political issue in affordability, but many of their preferred remedies would add costs rather than reduce them. Fixing the problem would require reconsidering policies they have spent years defending.

Worse, they increasingly want to impose those policies nationally, exporting mistakes made in high-cost blue states to places that have so far avoided them.

Yes, affordability is a problem. But you do not solve a problem by putting the people who helped cause it in charge of fixing it.
