news.title: Gloria Steinem, Trailblazing Feminist Icon and Activist, Dies at 92
news.text:
“I don’t want to die saying but—” Steinem told Vanity Fair over Zoom from her Manhattan home earlier this year in a conversation about her final memoir, titled An Unexpected Life, scheduled for release on September 22. “We have the idea that our lives are planned in order to be worthwhile. And that may be true in some cases,” Steinem said. “But I think our ability to respond to and learn from the unexpected is really much more likely to be helpful.”
Steinem’s death was announced in a post on social media Thursday. "Yesterday, Gloria Steinem passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her. Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” it read. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor.”
The statement continued, “She spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing. She has welcomed hundreds of guests into her living room for Talking Circles, a tradition she insisted will continue long after she is no longer with us. As Gloria wrote in her forthcoming book, An Unexpected Life, ‘I have now lived for more than fifty years in this brownstone, in rooms that have witnessed lives before mine, and will know others after I am gone.’ This book, along with her commitment to her home becoming a center for social justice movements, are among the many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come. Gloria often quoted the adage: ‘The flap of a butterfly’s wing can change the weather hundreds of miles away.’
“Gloria loved the tradition of lighting signal fires on hills to light the way to the other side of the mountain. Lighting your own candle for Gloria makes you part of this global and celestial community circle.”
Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio on March 25, 1934 and rose to national prominence as a journalist in 1963 following her undercover exposé, “I Was a Playboy Bunny.” The piece, published in Show magazine, revealed the sexist working conditions waitresses endured at New York City’s Playboy Club.
Steinem used her newfound spotlight to advocate for female equality, becoming a face of the feminist movement for over half a century. During that time, Steinem co-launched Ms. magazine in 1972 and was involved with multiple organizations that championed women, including the National Women’s Political Caucus, Voters for Choice, and the Women’s Media Center. “I’m not sure I saw any of it coming,” she told VF earlier this year. “I grew up in the 1950s in post-war conservatism. It was supposed to be that women married and had more children to replenish the population, and we were probably going to live where we were born. None of those things turned out to be true for my life.”
Speaking to Vanity Fair back in 1992, Steinem admitted she had actually been slow to embrace feminism. “Until I was into my thirties I was stoutly maintaining I had not been discriminated against,” she said “with regret,” as reported by Leslie Bennetts. “There was a well of anger so deep I just did not want to talk about it. I had difficulty renting an apartment, because if I was a single woman I wasn’t financially reliable and if I was financially reliable I must be a call girl. I was having an almost impossible time getting serious journalistic assignments. I was certainly dealing with what we now call sexual harassment—but it was all so bad I just displaced it. I identified with every other group that was being discriminated against—the farm workers, the civil-rights movement—rather than other women in my situation.”
Steinem’s parents separated when she was ten, and she was left on her own to care for a mother with mental health issues. For several years, Steinem believed her childhood hadn’t left scars. “I had a midwestern bias against therapy,” she told VF in ‘92, “a kind of survivor’s pride. I understood it for other people, but to me it just always seemed sort of unnecessary.” After finding therapy and continuing to work on herself, Steinem realized, “It’s difficult for a neglected child, because it isn’t that there’s something wrong—it’s that there’s nothing.” She said that at the age of 57, she officially felt “burnt-out” from her usual means of coping with her complex feelings. “You experience it as a lack of reality, as invisibility. So I set about making myself real by being useful.”
In addition to her philanthropic work and political advocacy, Steinem also had an impact on the world of pop-culture. She is largely regarded as “the woman who saved Wonder Woman,” after spending part of the 1960s advocating for the character of Diana Prince to regain use of her powers in the DC comics series. After that rightful restoration, Steinem featured Wonder Woman on the first issue of Ms. magazine in 1972. Steinem’s life was dramatized onscreen numerous times: first onstage in Emily Mann and Diane Paulus’s 2018 play Gloria: A Life; then on television in 2020 in FX’s Mrs. America (where she was played by Rose Byrne); and again later that year in director Julie Taymor’s decades-spanning The Glorias, in which Steinem was portrayed by Alicia Vikander and Julianne Moore, among others.
In 2000, Steinem, then 66, married lawyer David Bale. The union made her de facto stepmother to Oscar-winning actor Christian Bale, although she did not see it that way. “Christian is someone I met as a grown-up, so I think of him as a friend, not a stepson,” Steinem told The New York Times in September 2020. “It’s been a great gift to have David’s grown-up children as friends. And actually, completely without any work or deserving on my part, I have grandchildren!”
Steinem was “surprised” by the reaction that her marriage caused at the time. “There was disappointment from women I didn’t know,” she told the Times. “I mean, David and I loved each other and wanted to be together, and it turned out to be very important that we were together because only a year or so after we got married, he became ill. I think he needed someone to take him out of life.” Bale died of brain lymphoma in 2003. “His illness was a couple of years,” Steinem said, “being with him helped me acknowledge that it’s important to live in the moment.”
Steinem continued to play an active role in political life well after retirement age. She was front and center at the Women’s March in 2017, and remained vocal about the impact of the Trump administration, including the overturning of Roe v. Wade. A lifelong pro-choice advocate, Steinem remained passionate about American abortion access until the end of her life. “We either have power over our own bodies or we don’t have the most natural and intrinsic form of self-goverment,” she told Vanity Fair in March 2026. “As my old speaking partner, Florynce Kennedy, always said, ‘If men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament.’ We should be able to make decisions about our physical selves.” Steinem’s 2015 memoir, My Life on the Road, is dedicated to the doctor who performed her abortion at age 22, when the procedure was still illegal.
During that conversation, Steinem shared her optimism about future generations’ ability to carry the torch. “I definitely feel hopeful when I look at what women and men, mostly way younger than me, are doing,” she told VF. But Steinem had less enthusiasm for the man leading the country. “We in the United States don’t have a president we respect,” Steinem said when asked about the biggest threat Donald Trump posed. “One of the world’s most important democracies does not have a respected leader.”
Steinem endured two Trump presidencies, which were the result of Trump defeating female candidates Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. “When I am asked how I ‘still’ keep going—and I’m asked that a lot at my age,” a then 88-year-old Steinem told Vanity Fair in 2022, amid Joe Biden’s lone term as president, “I say it’s because action is infinitively interesting. You might be someone who knows the law and can help navigate legislatively. You might be a health care worker who can provide care and support, regardless of what the law says, or you might be really good at social media and spreading information and friendship. It’s rare that any one of us can solve a big problem, but collectively, we can do anything.”
Back at the Upper East Side brownstone apartment—“a symbol of the self,” as she wrote in My Life on the Road—where Steinem lived from 1967 until her death, she spent her final months devoted to service. In April of this year, she invited VF to visit her cozy, knick-knack-filled space for one of the discussion salons Steinem had hosted in her home for decades. “Though I used to be the youngest one in every circle, I now enjoy being the oldest one,” Steinem told the intimate group gathered around her living room, including this author. “And tell me how I can help.”
news.summary: The leader of the second-wave feminist movement dedicated her life’s work to advocating for women.

news.title: What happens when a blue state votes on trans sports?
news.text:
Republicans have been turning transgender athletes into a wedge issue since Idaho passed the first state ban in 2020. This year, it’s already playing a major role in midterm ads, with Democrats in competitive races almost always on the defensive. At this point, the fight doesn’t even need a trans athlete: The WNBA spent the summer at the center of a culture war over a hypothetical conflict, after two ex-NBA players declared themselves eligible for the women’s draft as a stunt. There have been no known trans women on any team, and the league confirmed it had “no immediate eligibility matters” on its hands. 

Key takeaways
* Twenty-seven Republican-controlled states have imposed measures to restrict trans athletes from playing in girls’ and women’s sports since 2020, but this year is the first time voters will have a chance to weigh in on the question directly.
* Washington state’s proposed measure to verify sex assigned at birth would apply to all girls seeking to play sports, not just players whose eligibility has been challenged.
* Democrats are split on how loudly to fight it. Washington’s congressional and legislative leaders oppose the measure, while the governor and both US senators have stayed quiet.

It became such a political priority in part because it polls well: Surveys show most Americans, including many otherwise Democratic-leaning voters, favor barring trans women from sports leagues. This November, though, marks the first time voters will confront the issue directly at the ballot box themselves.
Most notably, in Washington state, the public will decide whether to go further than any red-state legislature has even managed. A ballot initiative, I-638, would require every girl who wants to play school sports to first prove their sex assigned at birth, via an inspection of their reproductive anatomy or a test of their sex chromosomes or hormone levels. Competing campaigns in the state are mobilizing voters for and against the measure, which will deliver the clearest test yet of how liberal and moderate voters feel about this issue.
Twenty-seven other states have already imposed measures to restrict trans athletes from participating in girls’ and women’s sports in recent years, and the US Supreme Court ruled earlier this summer that such bans are constitutional. Yet nearly all of those bans passed through Republican-controlled legislatures, mostly in states Donald Trump won three times, and none went directly before voters. That changes this fall, not only in Washington but also with Arizona, Colorado, and Nebraska voters weighing in.
The blue-state ballot battle comes at a time when the Democratic Party is still struggling to figure out how it wants to talk about transgender athletes. Democrats have broadly supported anti-discrimination protections for trans people, but on the specific questions that have dominated the political debate — namely whether trans women and girls should play on sports teams matching their gender identity, and whether minors should have access to gender-related medical treatment — most Democrats have been reluctant to adopt clear positions, while some swing-state candidates have actively distanced themselves from the party.
But the Washington state referendum is forcing its opponents, and allied Democratic politicians, to tackle the issue head-on. And they think they may have found a way to win — by convincing even voters who agree with the ban’s goals that enforcing it will create more problems than it solves. 
What’s different about the Washington sports ban
The measure in Washington state is more far-reaching than other state bans in one key way, as it would require verification from every student seeking to join a girls’ sports team, not just those whose eligibility has been challenged. According to the text for I-638, athletes would need to document their sex assigned at birth based “only on one or more of the following: the student’s reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.”
Opponents, organizing under the banner of No Hate in WA State, are seeking to defeat the measure by framing it as the most extreme proposal of its kind. On paper, they face an uphill battle: 73 percent of Americans told Pew last year they were uncomfortable with transgender athletes playing on teams that don’t match their assigned birth sex. Opponents are also being massively outspent by Let’s Go Washington, the PAC campaigning for the measure, which is bankrolled by the conservative hedge fund manager Brian Heywood.
But No Hate in WA State hopes the ballot text will help them show that the proposed ban on transgender athletes would be a nightmare to implement. Even if Let’s Go Washington didn’t intend the outcome, they argue, no defensible reading of I-638 could avoid the conclusion that thousands of children will face either invasive new genital exams or the loss of a spot on a girls’ team altogether because their families can’t afford the genetic or testosterone testing the initiative offers as alternatives.
“Brian Heywood’s Initiative Wants To Inspect Your Daughter’s Body” reads a typical post from the No Hate in WA State campaign account, warning the initiative would yield “medically unnecessary” and “potentially traumatizing” genital or pelvic exams.
Let’s Go Washington disputes this, saying documentation of a genital exam from any routine past checkup, including the physical performed at birth, would suffice. But more than 150,000 school-age girls in Washington lack a regular family doctor with the medical records the campaign says would already be on file, and many schools conduct sports physicals publicly in group settings, where examining a student’s reproductive anatomy would be unthinkable.
Let’s Go Washington could not connect me with an attorney willing to defend its interpretation of the legislative text on the record, though campaign spokespeople Darren Littell and Hallie Herzberg said they consulted lawyers while crafting the ballot language. “I agree with you that it should have been explicit to say, ‘Here’s all the ways in the universe that you could verify a child’s sex’ and we didn’t do that, and that’s where we are now,” Herzberg told me.
Critics of the initiative warn the campaign will stir up more anti-trans sentiment and put vulnerable students in danger. The lead supporters say I-638 is necessary to protect the “integrity and fairness” of girls’ sports, and has nothing to do with targeting trans children. “This is not being motivated because we don’t like trans kids,” Littell said. “I’ve got family members who are trans, and I still love them and care about them.”
The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association is aware of about 10 transgender middle and high schoolers who play sports, out of more than 200,000 student-athletes statewide. Since 2007, the organization has allowed trans students to play on teams that align with their gender identity, with their handbook stating once a student-athlete is granted eligibility, they do not need to seek to renew eligibility every season or school year. 
“School sports is a place where kids can belong, a place of inclusion, where they can learn to work as a team and learn dedication,” Kelsey Gellner, a pediatric nurse based in Seattle, told me. “Tens of thousands of girls will be impacted by this to purposely exclude 10 children. That’s insane.”
Some opponents doubt the measure is really about protecting competition in female sports at all. Earlier this summer, the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with the Trump administration, released a report attacking Title IX, the federal law barring sex discrimination in federally funded schools and programs. The report argues for “unwinding our current regime” and blames the law for imposing a male model of competition on women, encouraging girls toward dominance and aggression, and pulling them away from femininity and motherhood.
“Preventing girls from playing sports is the whole point,” Megan Rapinoe, a two-time World Cup champion and Olympic gold medalist, wrote in a recent op-ed lambasting the ballot measure in Washington. “Spaces that leave girls and women feeling empowered are the spaces they want to constrict — and then eliminate.” 
Bringing adult restrictions down to children
The initiative’s proponents point to alternative means of verifying sex at birth, rather than genital exams. But hormone and genetic testing, the less invasive alternatives on offer, are very unusual for minors, and typically have only been required for certain elite adult athletes. 
Earlier this summer, for example, the Women’s Tennis Association announced it would require all players to undergo genetic sex testing in order to compete on the WTA Tour, a move that came on the heels of World Athletics requiring the same for participation in the female category for world ranking competitions. The goal would be to provide blood, saliva, or a cheek swab to test for any presence of the gene associated with the Y chromosome.
These tests are expensive, though, and require specialized training that public school staff virtually never have. 
“The language in the [Washington state] measure is quite alarming because it quite literally would codify sex testing for youth athletes into law,” Anna Posbergh, a professor at the University of Illinois Department of Recreation, Sport, and Tourism, told The Cut.
I-638 doesn’t specify how these tests would work in practice or who would pay for them. The ballot measure is also silent on intersex students, whose anatomy, chromosomes, and hormones may not point to the same answer. Littell says they would leave these questions “up to the doctors and patients, and at the end of the day this is common sense.” 
I asked the Washington State Medical Association what share of primary care and family medicine practices in the state could even run genetic or hormone testing in-house, and what referrals would look like for a rural practice.
“We don’t have that level of data, unfortunately,” Graham Short, a spokesperson for WSMA, told me. He added that his association does not yet have a formal position on the ballot measure, though their policymaking delegation convenes in September and may formulate a stance then. 
The Washington State Nurses Association has come out against the proposal. Gellner, who sits on its board, said it’s been disturbing to watch the idea of sports physicals shift from checking whether a student is healthy to play — i.e., checking their muscles, joints, blood pressure, and signs of asthma — to determining “whether the child themselves is a risk.”
The state chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, which has not taken a formal position, asked Let’s Go Washington to stop invoking the national group in the state’s official voter pamphlet, where the campaign cites AAP guidelines on routine childhood checkups. (The campaign refused.) Dr. Erica Li, a Spokane-based pediatrician who has been Let’s Go Washington’s most vocal physician in support of the measure, insisted to me that the process outlined in I-638 just “does not pose any barriers to any female” looking to participate in school sports.
Yet other states have backed away from language like this. A 2021 Florida law signed by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis originally had language saying that students would have to undergo a genital exam or get hormone or genetic testing if there were ever disputes over a student’s eligibility. That language sparked major controversy and was ultimately stripped from the final bill. House Republicans in Ohio also passed a bill in 2022 that would have required any student athlete whose sex was disputed to prove their sex assigned at birth through those same three options. After backlash, lawmakers removed the language from the Senate version, and put in a birth certificate requirement instead. 
A time of Democratic hesitance
Democrats have broadly supported anti-discrimination protections for trans people, but on sports specifically, the party has struggled to find agreement.
The Biden administration proposed a Title IX rule in 2023 that would have rejected blanket bans but allowed schools to restrict trans athletes’ participation in some cases, but the president never spoke about this nuanced rule publicly. Kamala Harris’s presidential campaign didn’t raise trans rights either, even as Republicans made them a centerpiece of their attacks against her. 
Democratic strategists have urged candidates to address transgender-related attacks more directly this time, but that hasn’t translated to a policy consensus. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger spent millions on ads acknowledging concerns about fairness and safety in school sports, for example, although even Spanberger’s actual position on the subject remains vague. 
Nationally, as the New York Times recently reported, Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts appears to be the only high-profile Democrat “eagerly campaigning as a supporter of transgender rights” this cycle.
In Washington state, some prominent Democrats have come out against I-638, including five Democratic members of Congress, such as Rep. Suzan DelBene, chair of the House Democratic Caucus, and Rep. Pramila Jayapal, who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus. The state’s top two legislative leaders, Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen and House Speaker Laurie Jinkins, have also come out against it. Gov. Bob Ferguson and Sens. Patty Murray and Maria Cantwell, though, have not publicly joined them. 
Polling thus far is unclear. A September 2025 poll of Washingtonians found 69 percent statewide support for the school-sports initiative, although the survey used language highly favorable to the measure, describing it as protecting “integrity and fairness” and did not explicitly say it would bar transgender girls from girls’ teams. 
No Hate in WA State referred me to May polling conducted by the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, a progressive group that tracks state ballot measures. Their survey rated I-638 a toss-up, finding voters sharply divided, with 43 percent strongly in favor, 21 percent strongly opposed, 17 percent fully undecided, and another 11 to 14 percent not firmly committed. BISC said they did not have more recent polling to share.
The measure, however it ultimately goes at the ballot box, will be a verdict on how the issue is playing out beyond red states, and directly with voters. For the handful of trans students the WIAA knows about, and for every other girl who wants to play sports, November will decide something more immediate. Voter pamphlets go out October 1.

news.title: Laura Loomer Brands Another Democrat a ‘Ghetto Black Communist B****’
news.text: Laura Loomer has used the same inflammatory language that sparked backlash over comments about Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon to target another Democratic lawmaker, just days after former Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene publicly condemned her remarks as racist. The right-wing activist on Wednesday directed a new attack at Representative LaMonica McIver of New Jersey, calling the Democrat a "ghetto black communist b****" in a post on X. The post came as Loomer continued to face criticism over similar remarks aimed at Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon. In that dispute, Loomer also mocked Nixon's speech as "Ebonics" and said she needed her "leash" tugged, comments that prompted condemnation from Greene and others. Newsweek has reached out to Loomer and McIver for comment and is awaiting responses. What Did Laura Loomer Say About Black Women? After calling Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon a "ghetto black communist b****" earlier this week, Loomer again used the same comment, this time aimed at McIver, writing on X: "LaMonica McIver is another ghetto black communist b**** who doesn’t belong in Congress." It was not long before McIver hit back on X, saying that she prayed Loomer would get "the help she so deeply and desperately needs." Loomer's remarks quickly drew attention online because they closely mirrored the language that had already generated controversy in the Nixon dispute. Laura Loomer Previously Defended Nixon Comments The latest exchange comes just days after Loomer refused to back down from her comments about Nixon. After receiving criticism, Loomer wrote on Sunday: "Is she ghetto? Yes. Is she black? Yes. Is she a communist? Yes. I spoke the truth." The remarks were widely criticized online and prompted a rare rebuke from Greene, who said she "1000 percent" denounced the comments and described them as racist. Greene also argued that such rhetoric was politically damaging and questioned why Loomer continues to maintain influence within President Donald Trump's political orbit. What Were LaMonica McIver Charges? McIver represents New Jersey in Congress and has become a frequent target of conservative criticism over immigration and law enforcement issues. Loomer's latest comments referenced federal charges stemming from a confrontation outside the Delaney Hall immigration detention facility in Newark in May 2025. Prosecutors allege McIver assaulted and interfered with federal officers during a clash that unfolded as Democratic Newark Mayor Ras Baraka was being arrested. McIver has pleaded not guilty and has repeatedly described the prosecution as politically motivated. The case remains ongoing. Last month, a federal appeals court largely rejected McIver's effort to have the charges dismissed, ruling that two of the counts can proceed and clearing the way for a trial. McIver had argued that she was protected by the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause because she was conducting congressional oversight at the facility. The court disagreed, although one charge was sent back to a lower court for further review. McIver responded to the ruling by saying "this is not over" and indicated she was exploring further legal options. Loomer's Controversial Comments The latest post suggests Loomer is not retreating from the rhetoric that sparked controversy over the weekend. Despite criticism from Democrats and Republicans, including a public rebuke from Greene, the activist has continued to defend her comments about Nixon and has now used similar language to target another Democratic lawmaker. Greene's condemnation was also notable because it was not the first time she has publicly broken with Loomer. In 2024, Greene criticized Loomer over comments about then-Vice President Kamala Harris that were widely condemned as racist, saying at the time that the remarks did not represent Republican values. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Rebecca Flood and James Debens
news.summary: Activist Laura Loomer targeted Democratic Representative LaMonica McIver after backlash over comments about Angie Nixon.

news.title: The 5 Most Heated Moments From Stephen A. Smith’s Sit-Down With Jemele Hill and Cari Champion
news.text:
It was the sports media reunion everyone was waiting for — and it delivered every bit of the drama promised. Stephen A. Smith pulled up to Cari Champion and Jemele Hill’s Flagrant and Funny podcast for a highly anticipated sit-down with his former ESPN colleagues.

​From the opening minute, sparks flew as accusations, long-held grievances, and deep-seated industry truths were laid out on the table in the first part of the three-hour interview.

​Here are the five most heated moments from the interview.

Stephen A. and Cari Clash Over Who Built Her Career at ESPN

​Tensions flared between Smith and Champion over her ESPN tenure. Smith publicly took credit for her First Take hiring, claiming she built her profile through his endorsement and positioning himself as the catalyst for diversity at the network. Champion flatly rejected his narrative, denying that Smith drove her success, calling out his alleged lies, and framing her career as entirely self-made. In the exchange about her time as the moderator of First Take, Smith said, “Skip Bayless did not want to hire you.”

​Champion replied: “Neither did you.”Smith went on to say, “You wanted the job at ‘SportsCenter.’ You wanted to come back.” 

“That is not true, Stephen A. I know you lying. That is not true. We are disagreeing right now,” Champion added.

RELATED: 5 Times That Stephen A. Smith Crossed The Line

Addressing “Same Smoke” Allegations Regarding White vs. Black Media Colleagues

​Champion and Hill also held Smith to the fire for his commentary, specifically comparing how aggressively he goes after Black female commentators compared to white former colleagues. They pressed him on why he went so hard at them and figures like Jasmine Crockett, Joy Reid, and even Michelle Obama on his podcast, while offering far softer responses or avoiding direct conflict with Michelle Beadle when she criticized him.

​Protecting Black Women vs. Corporate Self-Preservation

​While Smith argued that he was the driving force behind ESPN’s decision to hire more Black voices and give Black women top-tier shows on the network, Champion and Hill forced him to answer for the times they felt unsupported when corporate leadership squeezed them out. For Champion and Hill, authentic advocacy is measured not only by opportunities, but by solidarity when execs try to minimize them. Hill then criticized Smith for hypocrisy, noting that despite his rule of talking directly to colleagues before addressing them publicly, he backed ESPN in a Washington Post interview during her 2017 suspension for calling Donald Trump a racist without calling her first. Even Will Cain, a conservative commentator, gave her a heads-up about what he said.

“During that entire time, you never called me, you didn’t reach out and say ‘Hey, sis, you good?’ And I didn’t have that expectation of you,” Hill said.

Called Out Smith For Saying He Was Embarrassed For Voting For Kamala Harris

​Champion and Hill questioned Smith over his right-wing-leaning political commentary and his public statements that he felt like a “damn fool” and was embarrassed for voting for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. 

“I supported her leading up to the election. I voted for her. I was on the airwaves talking about what it was going to take to win,” said Smith.

While Smith said he had the right to offer his opinion on Harris’s performance, Champion and Hill challenged his rhetoric, questioning why he chose to publicly trash the Vice President after her defeat instead of offering a nuanced critique.

​Smith Speaking on NABJ Controversy On Sean Hannity’s Show

​After receiving the NABJ’s “Thumbs Down Award” for his commentary about Black women, Smith appeared on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show to defend himself. Champion and Hill challenged Smith’s decision to use Hannity’s platform. “Why Hannity?” Champion and Hill asked. They went on to challenge Smith, arguing that taking grievances against Black journalists onto Fox News — a network they say has been historically hostile to Black people — amplifies conservative talking points at the expense of Black institutions
news.summary:
In a heated discussion, the three prominent sports journalists aired out their disagreements in a highly anticipated episode of Flagrant and Funny.

news.title: Maple Grove is growing. Is it also turning blue?
news.text:
Warren Limmer left Maple Grove Republicans scrambling. 

After more than 30 years in the state Senate, the GOP lawmaker retired in February, right before the legislative session began. “It was a real shock to the community,” Limmer said in a phone interview. “No one was expecting me to retire.”

Limmer said he did minimal recruiting for his replacement to represent District 37, which also represents smaller towns to the west of Maple Grove, including Medina, Corcoran and Greenfield. 

A handful of Republican lawmakers informally asked state Rep. Kristin Robbins, R-Maple Grove, to vie for the seat. But Robbins was campaigning for governor until May.

Into the breach stepped Brady Hoag, a political neophyte with a work history as a corporate headhunter. 

“Brady was the only candidate who was seeking endorsement,” Limmer said. “He certainly did a lot of campaigning and worked hard to get the attention of delegates.”

After winning the party endorsement and primary, Hoag is up against Kristy Janigo, the DFL nominee who works for Hennepin County and touts her experience helping veterans. 

Maple Grove’s population has soared 50% since 2000 to about 74,000 residents. 

Related: Democrat Jake Johnson, a teacher, tries to solve the difficult math in a red district

The city’s The Shoppes at Arbor Lakes is a time capsule to a pre-Amazon era when midsized Midwestern municipalities had vibrant malls. And national companies including Boston Scientific have recently opened regional hubs in the city. 

As people and money have poured in, Maple Grove’s politics have, by some indications, moved to the left. District 37 voters went for Kamala Harris and Tim Walz over Donald Trump and JD Vance in the 2024 presidential election.

On the other hand, if Limmer ran again he would likely be the Kalshi betting favorite to win. Limmer garnered 55% of the vote in 2022. 

Here is what to look for in this state Senate race, which is one of a handful that could tilt party control in the Legislature.

Who is Kristy Janigo?

Janigo spent six years with the North Dakota National Guard and leads with her commitment to veterans. She is the legislative chair for two veterans nonprofits and was a Hennepin County veterans service officer for three years.

This includes working with lawmakers like Sen. Aric Putnam, DFL-St. Cloud, on funding to provide free meals to veterans. It also entails helping people make claims with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. 

“I’d literally go into people’s homes,” Janigo said during an interview at the Richfield Veterans of Foreign Wars post. “I worked with homeless veterans, so I’d go meet them out at a coffeeshop or at a Legion post.”

Related: Here are the races that will likely determine party control at the Minnesota Legislature

“Some veterans couldn’t deal with things on their own, like they couldn’t digitally sign documents,” she added. “So, I needed to come to them to collect their signatures in person.”

Janigo has worn an array of hats. She worked on product design for Target and later got a doctorate from the University of Minnesota in sustainable design. 

Janigo served as a faculty member in the fashion department of Arts Institute International Minnesota, the since shuttered Minneapolis college. 

She later pivoted into the public sector and since January has been doing site inspections and financial audits of behavioral health providers who get Hennepin County contracts. 

This experience, Janigo argued, is directly relevant to the pressing issue of Medicaid and child care providers accused of defrauding the state of Minnesota. “I’m literally doing the work on the frontlines to prevent waste and fraud,” she said.

If elected state senator, Janigo said she would like to pass a law that would make it easier to liquidate real estate assets from convicted fraudsters. 

Janigo is also a member of the Maple Grove City Council, where she has so far unsuccessfully pushed for community engagement liaisons with the city’s police department. She did help establish the role of city forester, who oversees Maple Grove’s two tree preservation areas.

Janigo floated one day combining these two interests. 

“I really like public safety so someday maybe I’ll be a natural resources cop or something,” Janigo said. “I’m interested in a lot of things.” 

Who is Brady Hoag?

Hoag has spent his career in the private sector, helping corporations including Wells Fargo recruit executive talent into Minnesota. He currently is a Minnesota-based partner for the Carlson Group, an executive search firm based in Des Moines.

Like Janigo, Hoag has spent years in Maple Grove and has a pronounced Minnesota accent. At an August debate in the City Council chambers of Maple Grove’s gleaming City Hall, Hoag declared, “I’m running because I believe our state is not heading in the right direction.”

He specifically noted that the state is running a structural deficit, which means spending is now outpacing revenue. (Outgoing Walz administration officials would surely reply that Minnesota, nonetheless, still has a $3 billion or so budget surplus). 

Hoag also claimed at the debate, held by the North Metro Mayors Association, that Minnesota is a “case study in fraud mismanagement that gets studied in board rooms and business schools across the country.”

The line got applause, though Hoag did not elaborate. 

Hoag declined to comment for this story. A campaign spokesperson said he is staying focused on voter interactions. 

Troy Olsen, government relations consultant for the North Metro Mayors Association, said Hoag is a bit of a mystery to some District 37 voters, because, unlike Janigo, he has not previously held public office. 

Limmer expressed confidence in his Republican heir. 

“He is very knowledgeable of the relationship between government and business,” Limmer said. “And I think I can say that he is very concerned about the job market in the state of Minnesota.”

Asked if he differed from Hoag on any issues, Limmer replied, “We really haven’t had that detailed of a discussion about issues, besides taxes and affordability.”

Robbins also praised Hoag, stating that she has gotten to know the candidate and his wife, Laura Hoag, over the last few months. “He is a terrific candidate who works hard, connects well with people, and understands what voters in our district want,” Robbins said.

What do voters in the district want?

Unlike District 3, whose tourism and mining economies face a profoundly uncertain future, or District 41 east of the Twin Cities, where concern lingers over safe drinking water, there is not an overarching issue bedeviling District 37.

The biggest concern expressed by voters I chatted with after the debate were congestion and construction.

Hoag said at the debate that he wants funding taken away from public transit projects like the Blue Line extension and put toward highways. 

Janigo said she would like to see the state adopt recommendations from the I-94 Corridor Coalition, a group representing local governments from Maple Grove west to St. Cloud. She also wants to explore bus rapid transit.

Janigo said at the debate “that the issues I hear the most about are affordability and fraud,” which Hoag also mentioned as his two key issues.

Besides laws that might help liquidate assets from fraudsters, Janigo also called for more site visits to social service providers and careful implementation of the state’s new Office of Inspector General, a hyped office that is unlikely to have jurisdiction over the Department of Human Services. 

Hoag suggested firing people who knew about the fraud.

Hoag’s affordability policies include using available state mechanisms to lower property taxes, and conformity with a temporary federal law that ends taxes on tips and overtime. 

Janigo mentioned finding ways to lower the cost of health care, something Minnesota is traditionally good at, though some solutions would involve cooperation with the Trump administration. 

Editor’s note: This story has been updated throughout to correct that Janigo was the legislative chair for veterans nonprofits, worked with Hennepin County veterans, helped people make claims with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and began work with behavioral health providers in January.
news.summary:
An open state Senate seat pits candidates with two starkly different backgrounds in a district long represented by GOP stalwart Warren Limmer.

news.title: MORNING GLORY: 'Blue Blight' is spreading fast and only voters can stop it
news.text: "Blue blight" is spreading across northeastern and west coast America, with scattered outbreaks in the interior of the country like Illinois and Colorado. It is up to voters to stop its spread. "Blue blight" isn’t a term-of-art yet. But, it will be. Consider that Dutch Elm Disease wasn’t a term familiar to Americans in the 1920s either. The devastating fungus arrived in the United States in the early 1930s and notably impacted a handful of Elm trees in Cleveland, Ohio. By the end of the 1970s, the Elms that had defined the Courthouse Square of my hometown of Warren as well as my own street, and, indeed, all of northeast Ohio were almost all gone. The fungus spread far and wide beyond Ohio, leaving a trail of felled tree stumps in its wake. To this day, it remains a threat to the remaining Elm population in the United States, even after it killed three out of four Elms across the country, and almost all of them in some places like northeastern Ohio. CALIFORNIA CONTROLLER CANDIDATE SLAMS MASSIVE EDUCATION SPENDING DESPITE WORSE STUDENT RESULTS The impacts of "blue blight" are becoming as visible as that of Dutch Elm Disease. Those impacts are most noticeable, to cite just two examples, in decreases in the quality of public education and declines in manufacturing jobs, even as state and local taxes rise. The second order impacts are now being felt across universities and colleges in states that are considered "blue." Kudos to The Wall Street Journal’s Douglas Belkin and Roshan Fernandez for their August 29 article titled "Why Syracuse Can’t Attract the Students It Needs to Pay the Bills." Kudos as well to Mary Katharine Ham and Vic Matus of the "Getting Hammered" podcast for some interesting speculation, prompted by the work of Belkin and Fernandez, on how the smaller number of college students — just the demographics of the decade ahead — are going to be looking beyond their choice of college to the job market and cost-of-living in the area surrounding their future campus and factoring those variables into their enrollment decision. Ham and Matus commented that perhaps students are going to tilt south to states like Florida rather than north to New York if they are looking at life choices ahead. Life choices as in "here are the jobs" and "what’s it cost to live in that state long term?" THE REAL REASON AMERICANS ARE FLEEING BLUE STATES FOR FLORIDA AND TEXAS I checked the numbers that are available against their thesis and, indeed, the available stats back them up. Using the data available from the Department of Education’s National Center for Education Statistics for the years 2017-2022 (the latest available) "blue states" — those that voted for then Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 — experienced substantially faster enrollment decline in higher ed than red states. NEW YORK CITY'S DECLINING PUBLIC SCHOOL ENROLLMENT PROJECTED TO LOSE OVER 150K MORE AS POPULATION DECLINES Of the six states that saw enrollments rise in their colleges and universities, five are "red": Georgia, Kentucky, Arizona, Indiana and Utah. Some deep red states did poorly (Alaska and Iowa) but the overall trend is there. Another factor to check on: manufacturing jobs. CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS When I first moved to California in 1978, its population was about 22 million souls and the state was home to close to 2 million manufacturing jobs. The Golden State’s population is today a half million shy of 40 million, but its total of manufacturing jobs has not simply failed to keep up with the population growth; the number of manufacturing jobs has actually plummeted to 1.2 million. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION How does that happen? "Blue blight." Another data point. California had 23 refineries in 2000. It is home to 11 today. Over 40 years, the refining output in the state has dropped by a million barrels a day. California motorists are paying about far more per gallon than red state residents. The cost in Indiana is several dollars a gallon cheaper. "Blue blight" claims victims in many ways but nowhere more than among those who consume energy. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Voters get the laws and regulations they vote for, and they can change or stay the course their home states are on. No doubt some citizens prefer the blue abyss ahead for high tax/high regulation states. But all voters get to choose. And they get to change their minds if the spread of "blue blight" alarms them. Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting. This column previews the lead story that will drive his radio/ TV show today. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM HUGH HEWITT

news.title: US House Rejects Bid to Limit Supreme Court to Nine Justices
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The US House of Representatives has rejected a Republican-backed effort to permanently set the number of Supreme Court justices at nine, amid a broader political debate over the court’s conservative majority.According to Al Jazeera, the proposal failed to secure the two-thirds majority required for a constitutional amendment, with lawmakers voting 212 in favor and 206 against. The vote largely followed party lines, with North Carolina Democrat Don Davis the only Democrat to support the measure.What Happened in the House Vote?Republicans introduced a joint resolution that would have amended the US Constitution to permanently limit the Supreme Court to nine justices.The proposal fell well short of the two-thirds support required for constitutional amendments. By contrast, ordinary legislation generally requires only a simple majority in the House.The vote came a day after the House approved a resolution condemning socialism by 220-192, with eight Democrats joining Republicans.House Speaker Mike Johnson criticized Democrats who opposed both measures, arguing that supporting the Constitution and defending the Supreme Court should not be controversial.Republicans' efforts have been viewed largely as political messaging ahead of the November midterm elections, seeking to put Democrats on record over issues including socialism and possible expansion of the Supreme Court.Why Is the Supreme Court’s Size Being Debated?The debate stems partly from calls by some Democrats to expand the Supreme Court in response to its conservative majority.The idea, often called “court packing” by opponents, gained renewed attention after former President Donald Trump appointed three justices during his first term. The conservative-leaning court subsequently delivered several legal victories to Trump.In 2021, four Democratic lawmakers introduced legislation that would have expanded the Supreme Court to 13 justices. They argued that the move would restore balance to the court after what they described as Republican efforts to reshape the judiciary.More recently, Democratic Senator Jim Clyburn of South Carolina backed the idea of a 13-member court, while former Vice President Kamala Harris said Democrats should have a serious discussion about expanding the court.Republicans have strongly opposed such proposals, arguing that changes could undermine the independence of the federal judiciary.Does the US Constitution Set the Number of Justices?No. Although the Constitution establishes the Supreme Court, it does not specify how many justices must sit on the court.Congress has therefore determined the court’s size through legislation over the country's history.The Judiciary Act of 1789 initially established a six-member Supreme Court, consisting of a chief justice and five associate justices. The number changed several times during the 19th century before Congress set the current number of nine justices in 1869.That history means the number of Supreme Court seats is not constitutionally fixed and can be changed by Congress without amending the Constitution.Has the Supreme Court Been Expanded Before?Yes. The size of the Supreme Court has changed several times since its creation.The most famous modern attempt to expand the court came from President Franklin D. Roosevelt after he won reelection in 1936.Roosevelt proposed adding justices based on the age of sitting members, potentially allowing up to six additional justices. The plan became known as the “court-packing” proposal and faced strong opposition.More recently, groups including the Brennan Center for Justice have advocated structural reforms such as term limits and ethics rules, while some Democratic lawmakers have continued to support expanding the court.The issue has now returned to the political spotlight as the United States approaches another closely watched midterm election.Read: US Supreme Court Allows Trump Ballroom Project to ProceedClick here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News

news.title: Donald Trump Beats Zohran Mamdani on Net Favorability: New Poll
news.text: President Donald Trump has a more favorable net favorability rating than New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, according to a new Harvard CAPS/Harris poll, though both men are underwater among voters as two of the most recognizable faces of their respective parties. Trump has a net favorability rating of -8 percent, with 42 percent of registered voters viewing him favorably and 50 percent unfavorably, according to the poll. Mamdani, meanwhile, has a net favorability rating of -14 percent, with 25 percent viewing him favorably and 39 percent unfavorably. The poll surveyed 2,100 registered voters from August 28-30, 2026, and has a margin of error of 2.1 percent. The numbers are notable because Trump and Mamdani have become defining figures for the Republican and Democratic parties, respectively. Trump has reshaped the GOP around his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, while Mamdani's rapid rise has made him one of the most prominent figures associated with the Democratic Party's progressive wing. Newsweek reached out to the White House and Mamdani's office via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know The Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll found that 51 percent of voters believe the Democratic Party is being taken over by the far left, while 45 percent believe the Republican Party is being taken over by the far right. Mamdani's rise has nevertheless represented a significant shift within the Democratic Party. His progressive agenda and upset victory over establishment Democrat Andrew Cuomo in New York's mayoral primary have made him a national political figure, while also fueling debate over whether Democrats should embrace his brand of politics or distance themselves from it. Trump faces a similar dynamic on the Republican side, where his continued dominance has made it somewhat difficult for the party to separate itself from his agenda and political style. The result is a striking political paradox: Trump and Mamdani may be among the clearest faces of America's increasingly polarized parties, but neither is viewed favorably by a majority of Americans, according to the new poll. As both parties look toward the 2026 midterm elections, the question may be whether voters want more of the political movements these two men represent—or something different altogether. Grant Davis Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek via email on Wednesday, "This probably reflects the fact that President Trump and the Republicans have made socialism and Mamdani a central target of their negative messaging in recent weeks. It’s having an effect, apparently." "Mamdani is also actually making changes, and has had some glitches with staff, etc., and as those mount that will take some shine off of the 'young phenom' effect he’s been enjoying. But that doesn’t explain the national numbers, because most Americans don’t follow day-to-day policy and politics in NYC," he added. When asked if Americans view both Trump and Mamdani as leaders of their party, Reeher later said, "The president is always the de facto leader of his party. Trump is no different, but there are divisions within the ranks, on both the Iran war and the tariffs. I don’t see Mamdani as the recognized 'leader' of the Democratic Party, and doubt he ever will be. He’s one of the principal leaders of the Left wing of the party, that’s for sure. I don’t think the party has a particular leader at the moment, to be honest." Florida Atlantic University politics professor Craig Agranoff also told Newsweek on Wednesday when asked about the net favorability numbers, "A month-to-month flip like this is not shocking." "National favorability for both men moves with the news cycle, and Mamdani is still building name recognition outside New York. Trump remains far better known, so his numbers are more settled even when they sit underwater. That does not make either man the uncontested leader of his party. Trump is still the central figure on the Republican side because he occupies the White House and defines the coalition," Agranoff added. "Mamdani is a rising face of the Democratic left, but the party still has multiple power centers and he does not yet speak for the whole national brand. Favorability gaps this size tell you more about visibility and polarization than about who actually runs either party." Meanwhile, the Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll shows only two U.S. political figures with positive net favorability: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump's net favorability in the poll is worse than former Vice President Kamala Harris, Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and House Speaker Mike Johnson. The poll shows Trump's net favorability is better than California Governor Gavin Newsom, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Tucker Carlson and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan. What Polls Show Other polling, however, has shown that Mamdani's favorability has been positive as he has settled into office. An early-August Siena College poll found 47 percent of New York likely voters viewed him favorably, compared with 44 percent who viewed him unfavorably, while other polling around his first 100 days in office showed 48 percent of New Yorkers approving of his performance and 30 percent disapproving. July's Harvard CAPS/Harris poll showed Trump's net favorability at -13 percent, with 40 percent net favorability compared to 53 percent net unfavorability. The poll showed Mamdani with a net favorability of -7 percent, with 27 percent net favorability and 35 percent net unfavorability. That poll surveyed 1,776 registered voters from July 11-12, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.3 percent. A Siena University poll taken in June showed Trump's favorability at 32 percent, compared with 63 percent unfavorable. The survey showed that Mamdani's favorability was positive, at 45 percent, compared to 34 percent unfavorable. The poll surveyed 1,120 New York State registered voters from June 17-23, 2026, and had a margin of error of 3.6 percent. A May Harvard CAPS/Harris poll showed that Trump's net favorability was -6 percent, with a 43 percent net favorable rating compared to 50 percent net unfavorability. Mamdani's net favorability rating was 23 percent compared to a net 33 percent unfavorable rating. Mamdani's overall net favorability in the poll was -10 percent. The poll surveyed 1,725 registered voters from May 29-31, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.4 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas

Yet according to one expert, Democrats will not have an easy job gaining control of that legislative chamber, despite their seeming advantages.

"President Donald Trump’s low job approval ratings, coupled with large Democratic leads in generic congressional polling, have most analysts expecting the House to flip to team blue in November," wrote Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center, for The Washington Post on Wednesday. "That’s still the most likely outcome, but a seat-by-seat analysis reveals a tougher challenge for Democrats than the overall picture suggests."

Olsen began by pointing out the raw numerical strength held by Republicans.

"Large midterm gains usually occur when the party in power loses seats that typically lean toward the other side. In 2018, Republicans held 25 House seats Hillary Clinton had carried two years earlier; they lost 22 of them," Olsen wrote. "But thanks to increased polarization (and mid-cycle redistricting shenanigans), the GOP only holds eight seats won by Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024."

He added, "Redistricting has also shifted the House map sharply in the GOP’s favor. The median House seat — the 218th seat required for House control — under the 2024 maps was Arizona’s 1st District, which Trump carried by 3.1 percentage points. Now it’s Virginia’s 1st District, which he won by 4.9 points. Winning that district plus every single House seat Trump carried by less than that will be a tall order."

On top of Democrats needing to win these swing districts, they will also need to pull off some upsets, which Olsen characterized as unlikely.

"No party ever sweeps all the seats a baseline partisan analysis suggests it can win," Olsen argued. "That means Democrats probably need to take a few of the seats above the median to secure control of the House. Those seats are demographically even tougher."

Ultimately, Olsen did not discount Democrats' advantages, but simply urged political observers to be cautious before overstating their chances of prevailing.

"Democrats have wind in their sails," Olsen concluded. "Trump is highly unpopular, and they have every reason to believe their voters will turn out for them. But that doesn’t mean House control is assured. Their path to a House majority runs through 2024 Trump voters, and convincing enough of them to switch allegiances won’t be easy."

Despite Republicans' non-zero chances of retaining both chambers, Trump has made it clear that he plans on meddling in the midterms. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine refused last month to rule out the possibility of sending the military to stop Democrats from winning, instead merely saying he "has no plans" to do so, and Trump has considered many other measures to intimidate Democrats from appearing at the polls.

“I think there are two things to consider,” Pooja Chaudhuri, Senior Counsel/Deputy Legal Director at Democracy Defenders Fund who specializes in voting rights as well as election law litigation and advocacy, told AlterNet in June. “One is that the election is made up of voters, and so the outcome depends on people turning out to the polls and voting. The problem is ... the chilling effect on voters.”

Chaudhuri continued, “When voters hear that ICE may be deployed to the polls, that mail-in voting rules are changing close to the election, a lot of voters might say, ‘I'm just not going to go out and vote.’ That could happen in many different ways. There are vulnerable communities — people may come from mixed-status families — they're US citizens, but they might decide, 'I'm not going to vote.' So one aspect is the chilling effect on voters that all of these actions would have.” Nor is that the only card Trump may play.

“We're going to see consequences in terms of voters saying, ‘I don't want the FBI to get my personal ballot in the future,’” Chaudhuri concluded. “So, to sum up, I do agree that putting it all together, it does paint an ominous picture.”

news.title: 1 in 6 Trump voters would change their 2024 vote, poll finds
news.text:
Nearly two years after Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris to win back the White House, some of the voters who helped put him there are having second thoughts.

A new University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov poll found that 16% of Trump voters say they would change their 2024 vote if given the chance. An even larger share, 21%, said they now have second thoughts about supporting the president.

The findings come as Trump's approval ratings remain underwater in multiple national surveys and amid concerns over the economy, rising prices and the ongoing war in Iran.

Why it matters

The poll, released Aug. 31, found that 57% of respondents believe Trump has performed worse than they expected since returning to office in 2025. The survey also showed Trump's approval rating at 32%, down one percentage point from the university's previous poll in April.

The results were released the same day a Reuters/Ipsos survey found Trump's job approval rating holding at 33% for a third straight week, marking his lowest rating in that poll since returning to office.

The University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov survey polled 1,000 respondents from Aug. 21-26 and has a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points.

Iran, inflation weigh on voters

The survey suggests voters remain frustrated by several issues facing the administration, particularly the ongoing conflict with Iran and rising consumer costs.

Only 26% of respondents said they approve of the war in Iran, and roughly 1 in 4 said they believe the United States is winning the conflict.

"With no end in sight to the ongoing war in Iran, the continued rise in the price of gas, groceries, utilities, and housing, an escalating trade war with Canada, and the likelihood of higher interest rates, it comes as no surprise that Trump's approval rating remains at a paltry 32%," Tatishe Nteta, director of the UMass Amherst Poll, said in a news release.

According to AAA, the national average price for a gallon of gas stood at $4.12 on Sept. 2, up 3 cents from a month earlier and nearly $1 higher than a year ago.

What do polling averages show?

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump in negative territory overall:

news.title: Two Dems clashed on trans athletes. What does Markey's primary win reveal?
news.text:
Rep. Seth Moulton was among the first Democrats after the 2024 elections to publicly question his party’s support for the inclusion of transgender athletes in sports. 

That decision, and the backlash that followed, likely contributed to his loss in Massachusetts' Sept. 1 primary against 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey.

Two years after Republicans made transgender rights a central focus of their 2024 election attack ads, Democrats are still working through how to message on an issue that is deeply important to their base, but polls poorly with much of the electorate.

Moulton, 47, centered his campaign on generational change and the need for new blood in Congress. But Markey was able to easily fend off the challenge by emphasizing his progressive platform, including support for transgender rights.

The senator contrasted his message with remarks Moulton made after Democrats lost up and down the ticket in the 2024 election, when Moulton told The New York Times that he didn’t want his two young daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete,” a comment Moulton said he was supposed to be “afraid to say" as a Democrat.

While Markey's progressive politics helped him in Massachusetts, Democrats competing outside the bluest states in the country are already facing a new wave of attacks ads on transgender rights, specifically regarding girls' and women's sports.

“There's no doubt in my mind that this is going to come up in every single race at every single level, and Democrats have to be prepared to respond,” said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at Third Way, a center-left think tank. “What we've seen is if people think that what the Republicans are saying is true, they think that Democrats are extreme.”

Markey took on Moulton's comments on trans athletes

During the 2024 presidential election cycle, Donald Trump’s campaign spent millions of dollars on ads attacking then-Vice President Kamala Harris for her stances on transgender rights, arguing that Harris was “for they/them” and Trump was “for you.” The president and his campaign said Harris also supported taxpayer funded gender affirming care for detainees, likely referring to a 2019 ACLU questionnaire where Harris agreed to ensure medical care for transgender and nonbinary people who "rely on the state - including those in prison and immigration detention."

After the election, Moulton and a handful of other prominent Democrats sought to push their party to have a debate over its stance on transgender athletes in girls sports. 

Markey made Moulton’s comments a focal point of his primary campaign. After the congressman announced his challenge, Markey appeared at a No Kings rally draped in a transgender pride flag. 

Moulton sought to pivot left on the issue during the campaign.

He signed onto the Transgender Bill of Rights in the House. At a debate last month, the congressman apologized for his comments to The New York Times and said transgender athletes “should” be able to participate in sports leagues that match their gender identity, with some safety qualifications. 

Markey said Moulton “threw those kids under the political bus after the election” and turned them into “political fodder.” 

Transgender athletes a topic in competitive states

Democrats are still weighing how to discuss transgender athlete participation in battleground races, where public opinion is likely less favorable. A 2025 Gallup poll found that 69% of Americans oppose allowing transgender athletes to play on the teams that match their gender identity, up from 62% in 2021. 

“The Democrats are never going to win on that issue,” said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist. “This is not a close call.”

Rob Sand, Iowa's Democratic nominee for governor, has been opposed to allowing transgender girls to participate in girls sports leagues throughout his campaign. Trump won Iowa in all three of his presidential campaigns, but the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the seat a Lean Democratic race. 

"I have said, consistently, I think that fairness rules the day in girls' sports,” Sand told Politico last month. "I just think girls' sports are for girls, and boys' sports are for boys. And I think that that's fair and reasonable."

Democrat Amy Acton, a former public health official running for governor in Ohio, said in June she doesn’t support “boys playing in girls sports” and would enforce the state’s ban on school age transgender athletes participating in sports. Equality Ohio, an LGBTQ rights group, changed her rating from A to pending as a result of her comments. 

Democrats have been most effective, Erickson said, when they say they want sports to be fair and safe, and support allowing sports associations to set the rules. Candidates have also had success noting that bans on transgender athletes can lead to invasive gender checks on children, she said.

Erickson and other Democratic strategists pointed to Abigail Spanberger’s successful 2025 Virginia gubernatorial campaign, in which she quickly responded to attacks on transgender rights from her Republican opponent and called on politicians to “trust parents and local communities” to set rules on transgender athlete participation. 

Tyler Hack, the executive director of the Christopher Street Project, a transgender rights group, said that in a blue state like Massachusetts allyship looks like Markey’s “unapologetic defense” of transgender rights.

But the organization is also working with candidates in tough races on how to talk about transgender athletes and other issues in ways that resonate with voters in their districts. 

“If candidates want to talk about this issue through a lens of local participation, and if that works for them, I have no problem with that. The problem is when you have candidates call transgender girls boys,” Hack said. “That is a hard line for our party, and last night should show that that's not where voters are.”

news.title: Kamala Harris Suffers Embarrassing 'Jeopardy!' Snub — as All 3 Contestants Are Left Stumped by Question About Ex-Veep

Jeopardy! contestants unintentionally dealt former Vice President Kamala Harris an embarrassing blow, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

Initial criticism mounted over the fact that Harris was not technically the Democratic Party nominee. However, the party was forced to rally behind her in the unprecedented move as they faced Donald Trump.

news.title: Voters Say They Want Younger Politicians. So Why Do They Keep Voting for Old Ones?
news.text:
Here’s a paradox for you: In overwhelming numbers, voters keep telling pollsters that they want upper age limits and term limits for members of Congress. At the same time, they keep voting to reelect long-serving lawmakers who are in their 70s and 80s.

Massachusetts offers the latest evidence. Older incumbents of all ideological stripes swept the state’s Democratic primaries last night. In the race for U.S. Senate, two-term Sen. Ed Markey, an 80-year-old progressive, easily dispatched the more moderate Rep. Seth Moulton, 47. Elsewhere, Reps. Richard Neal and Stephen Lynch, who are both in their 70s and have collectively been in office for more than six decades, fended off younger and leftier challengers.

So what’s really going on? Here are a few theories.

Ideology over age

As the saying goes, age is but a number. Yet voters keep telling us it’s actually a lot more than that. At first glance, Markey’s win would seem to break a recent streak of older incumbents falling to more youthful candidates. So far this year, the losers include Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York (71), Rep. Shri Thanedar of Michigan (71), and Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado (69). But Markey’s victory also fits a different pattern: In all three of those earlier races, the elder lawmaker lost to a more outspokenly progressive rival. And for Massachusetts Democrats contemplating who they wanted as their next senator, ideology was clearly more important than age.

When Moulton launched his campaign, he downplayed any real policy differences with Markey. “Sen. Markey is a good man, but it’s time for a new generation of leadership,” he said in his announcement video. Markey, though, hammered the issues where they did diverge—including the debate over transgender rights. After Kamala Harris lost in 2024, a defeat some Democrats attributed in part to a viral pro-Trump ad that argued “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you,” Moulton expressed opposition to trans athletes playing in women’s sports. “I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete,” he told the New York Times.

Moulton later retreated from those remarks (“I’m sorry if my comments hurt you,” he told the trans community last month), but Markey sought to make them stick. “Trans rights are human rights,” the senator said recently. In a preelection poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, two-thirds of likely Democratic primary voters said they were less likely to support a candidate who had opposed trans rights, and about the same share said they trusted Markey to better represent them on the issues they cared about. So going forward, it’s probably better to think of age as a factor, but rarely the factor, in how voters approach candidates.

The power of incumbency

Moulton’s drubbing has some progressives crowing that new ideas, not just fresh faces, are what Democrats need to compete. How, then, to explain the survival of Neal and Lynch, two longtime members of Congress who put down progressive challenges from first-time candidates last night?

One answer is straightforward: Politicians who seek reelection almost always win. Nationwide, 95 percent of all incumbents reclaimed their seats in 2024. Journalists have showered ink on the anti-establishment fervor that’s supposedly sweeping the Democratic Party, buoyed by voters furious over its longtime leaders’ failure to prevent Donald Trump’s return. But even in that treacherous environment, only seven sitting House Democrats have lost renomination so far this year, a tiny fraction of those running for reelection. Lynch and Neal both won relatively narrowly, which may suggest some frustration with their long tenures or more centrist records (or both). But there’s clearly a risk of overstating Democrats’ unhappiness with their party’s old guard—and of mapping that anger too neatly onto ideology.

Health, not age

Polling is an imperfect instrument, and asking voters whether they favor a given candidate or policy doesn’t always tell you why they feel the way they do. So another possible explanation for the apparent paradox over older politicians is that age, at least by itself, isn’t really what voters are worried about. The better term for what’s on their minds may instead be health, both cognitive and physical.

The clearest example is what happened last month, when Rep. John Larson, a 78-year-old Democrat who has represented Connecticut since 1999, lost his primary to a younger challenger. But Larson wasn’t just old and established. He had a complex partial seizure while delivering an on-camera speech on the House floor last year, stopping midsentence before continuing to speak in a slow and halting voice for more than 30 seconds. Larson’s office later attributed the seizure to a congenital heart issue, adding that he’d been prescribed medication to help. But it’s not all that shocking that voters declined to return him to Congress, opting instead for a 47-year-old former mayor who campaigned on generational change.

The health-over-age dynamic may also explain Markey’s resilience. As even some of Moulton’s supporters acknowledged, the 80-year-old senator still looks spry and sounds with it. (After a recent rally, Markey’s campaign blasted out video of the senator shooting hoops.) Markey would be 86 at the end of his next term, the same age Joe Biden would’ve been had he won and finished a second term, but voters evidently saw them differently. In a Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll last month, only a third of Massachusetts primary voters said Markey’s age made them less inclined to support him. When Biden launched his reelection bid, on the other hand, even most Democrats told pollsters that he was too old for another term. They may have been alarmed less by the year on Biden’s birth certificate and more by his apparent physical frailty, softening voice, and questions about his mental acuity.

OK, time to switch gears. For your evening enjoyment, why not:

Take a break with this movie review: We regret to inform you that Raygun is back. The Aussie breakdancer who went viral in 2024 for her cringingly bad performance at the Summer Olympics in Paris is the subject of an infuriating new Netflix documentary about the whole ordeal. Slate culture writer Nadira Goffe watched it so you don’t have to.

Soothe your inner child with some nostalgic tunes: When Rebecca Knight became a parent, she vowed that her kids wouldn’t listen to Raffi. But she quickly realized the error of her ways, thanks to a Laura Marling album of Raffi covers. (If you want to learn more about Raffi’s singular status in the world of kids’ music, listen to this 2023 episode of Working in which the artist breaks down his creative decisions.)

Get in the back-to-school spirit: It can be hard to adjust to the end of summer vacation. But there is one small part of the new school year that is guaranteed to enthrall students, parents, and teachers alike. Slate staff writer Heather Schwedel investigates why lamination—a hallmark of an organized classroom—has such a hold on both kids and grown-ups.

Give your brain a workout: Who is “Wonder Woman’s godly enemy” (four letters)? Which city “has a Jewish population that is neither Sephardic or Ashkenazi” (four letters)? Test your wordplay skills with today’s crossword.

Alas, writing this newsletter has exhausted my wordplay skills, so I’m off to walk the dog instead. Enjoy the rest of your night!
